project.name: ruby-gba
project.description: A Ruby DSL that compiles plain Ruby into real Game Boy Advance ROM files. Built as a teaching tool: the author should need to know Ruby, not the hardware. The DSL builds a target-agnostic IR op-tree, a validation pass turns known footguns into friendly build errors, and a backend either lowers it to ARM7 machine code or interprets it in Ruby as a headless test oracle.

nodes.name: ci.yml
nodes.summary: Manual-dispatch GitHub Actions workflow that provisions a compiler, libmgba and ImageMagick, then runs three checks in one job: the main Ruby suite, gemba-core's own headless-emulator suite, and the emitted-code baseline comparison. Every log is uploaded as an artifact even when a step fails.
nodes.languageNotes: Trigger is `workflow_dispatch` only — no build on push or PR — guarded by a per-ref concurrency group with cancel-in-progress. The apt step is what makes the emulator-backed tests possible: `libmgba-dev` supplies the system library that gemba-core's C extension links against, and because the probe is headless there is no SDL2, X11 or audio daemon to install. The Ruby matrix carries a single version ('4.0'), so it is scaffolding for future versions rather than real fan-out; `fail-fast: false` keeps one version's failure from cancelling the rest.

nodes.name: commit-msg
nodes.summary: Git commit-msg hook that rejects any commit message embedding a bead tracker id (the lowercase `gba-<id>` form), keeping internal issue-tracker state out of permanent git history.
nodes.languageNotes: POSIX sh; blanks out the project's own `ruby-gba` / `ruby-gba-emulator` names before scanning because grep here has no lookbehind and those names match the bead-id pattern exactly.

nodes.name: Gemfile
nodes.summary: Bundler manifest that pulls runtime dependencies from the gemspec and adds the vendored `ruby-gba-emulator` gem by path for development only, so consumers of the library never need a C compiler or libmgba.
nodes.languageNotes: A `path:` source puts the emulator on the load path but does NOT build its C extension — `rake compile_emulator` does that, and switching Ruby versions requires `rake clean` in the emulator directory.

nodes.name: LICENSE.md
nodes.summary: MIT license for the project, plus sections on trademarks and a warning about the Nintendo boot logo that a real GBA cartridge header requires.

nodes.name: README.md
nodes.summary: Project front door: pitches the Ruby-to-GBA-ROM DSL as a teaching tool written end-to-end by AI, then walks the design pillars (hide the hardware, guardrails, the value-centric DSL, the target-agnostic IR, effect packs, `rom.profile`), the feature-progress table, the example catalogue, and the project layout.

nodes.name: Rakefile
nodes.summary: Build and test orchestration: compiles the emulator's C extension as a cached file task, defines the serial `test` and parallel `test:parallel` suites with SimpleCov collation, and adds tasks for emitted-code baselines, HTML example previews, and the local knowledge-graph viewer.
nodes.languageNotes: The compiled extension is a Rake file task keyed on source mtimes, so it cannot notice a Ruby-version switch — a compiled extension is tied to the Ruby that built it, which is what `rake clean` in the emulator directory is for.

nodes.name: ruby-gba
nodes.summary: Executable entry point for the `ruby-gba` command line tool: puts `lib` on the load path so it runs from a checkout, then hands ARGV to `RubyGBA::CLI.start`.

nodes.name: animate.rb
nodes.summary: Example ROM demonstrating flipbook sprite animation: a spinning coin built from four generated frames cycled by `frames:`/`rate:`, steered around the field with the D-pad to show animation composing with movement.

nodes.name: Animate
nodes.summary: Module holding the coin's frame constants, the generated frame art, and the `RubyGBA.game` build block, exposing `program` and `build_rom` delegators used by the test suite and the ROM writer.

nodes.name: self.coin_art
nodes.summary: Generates one animation frame as ASCII art: a gold disc squashed horizontally to the frame's SPIN factor, so cycling the four frames reads as a coin turning edge-on and back.

nodes.name: gen_pacman_sheet.rb
nodes.summary: Asset-authoring script that bakes the disc-and-mouth formula from `examples/pacman.rb` into a real sprite sheet PNG, laid out as one row per direction and two columns (mouth open, mouth shut) for `sprite facing_from:` to import.
nodes.languageNotes: Shells out to ImageMagick (`magick`) to write the PNG — the same tool the framework's importer reads it back with.

nodes.name: yellow_rgb
nodes.summary: Converts the framework's `:yellow` from its 15-bit BGR555 value into 8-bit RGB channels, so art drawn into the sheet imports back as exactly the same yellow the formula produces.

nodes.name: level.csv
nodes.summary: A 30x20 tilemap exported in the CSV form a map editor like Tiled writes: one tile number per cell, 1 for brick walls and 2 for floor, imported by `examples/level.rb` via `background from:`.

nodes.name: bird.rb
nodes.summary: Example ROM importing a sprite straight from a native `.aseprite` file with no export step: a six-frame wing flap that also tilts with `face_angle` and breathes in and out with `pulse`.

nodes.name: Bird
nodes.summary: Module holding the bird's speed and pulse constants plus the `RubyGBA.game` build block, exposing `program` and `build_rom` delegators.

nodes.name: breakout.rb
nodes.summary: The bitmap-mode flagship showcase: a complete Breakout with paddle, ball, brick wall, score, three lives, scenes, sound and music, drawn double-buffered (`tear_free: true`) because the whole screen is repainted every frame.
nodes.languageNotes: Paddle and ball are plain variables drawn with `draw_rect_at` rather than sprites: a sprite earns its keep by saving and restoring the background under it, which is wasted when the frame clears and repaints everything anyway.

nodes.name: Breakout
nodes.summary: Module holding the game's build-time layout constants and the full `RubyGBA.game` block — title, playing, win and game-over scenes, brick collision, scoring and audio — plus the `program` and `build_rom` delegators.

nodes.name: buffered_bounce.rb
nodes.summary: Minimal tear-free demo: three balls bounce while the whole screen is cleared and repainted each frame, showing that `tear_free: true` alone removes the tearing that pattern causes on a direct-color screen.

nodes.name: BufferedBounce
nodes.summary: Module holding the screen constants and the `RubyGBA.game` block that bounces three rectangles on a double-buffered bitmap screen, plus the `program` and `build_rom` delegators.

nodes.name: corridor.rb
nodes.summary: First-person maze crawl that deliberately runs close to the per-frame budget: sixty rays cast through an 8x8 map, drawn as wall columns into a letterboxed `inside` view with a gold-counting status bar underneath.
nodes.languageNotes: The `inside` clip is what makes the status bar free: the rows under the view are never drawn rather than drawn and then covered, which on a near wall is most of a column.

nodes.name: Corridor
nodes.summary: Module holding the maze map, precomputed sine/cosine/gold tables and the whole first-person game, exposing `game`, `program` and `build_rom`.

nodes.name: self.game
nodes.summary: Builds the whole corridor ROM: declares the trig and gold tables and the player state, then per frame casts sixty rays through the map, draws each as a distance-shaded wall column inside the clipped view, handles turning and blocked movement, and updates the gold HUD.

nodes.name: floating_digits.rb
nodes.summary: Demo of moving text: the digits 0-9 drift and bounce off the screen edges, each rendered as a glyph image taken from the built-in font and `blit` at a runtime position, since `draw_text`/`draw_number` only draw at fixed spots.

nodes.name: FloatingDigits
nodes.summary: Module holding the screen and glyph metrics, one distinct color per digit, the glyph-art extraction from the default font, and the `RubyGBA.game` block that moves and blits all ten digits.

nodes.name: font_styles.rb
nodes.summary: Demo of user-defined fonts: the same word drawn in three faces, two of them declared inline in the build block with `font :name do … end` and selected per call with `draw_text font:`.

nodes.name: FontStyles
nodes.summary: Module whose `RubyGBA.game` block defines a rounded lowercase font and a slanted script font from glyph art, then draws the same word in each alongside the built-in 5x7 face.

nodes.name: fonts.rb
nodes.summary: Smallest font demo: the same score drawn once in the built-in 5x7 `:default` face and once in the compact 3x5 `:tiny` face, showing per-call font selection from the font registry.

nodes.name: FontsDemo
nodes.summary: Module holding the demo score and the `RubyGBA.game` block that draws it twice with different `font:` names, plus the `program` and `build_rom` delegators.

nodes.name: grid_cursor.rb
nodes.summary: Demo of the `grid` verb: a single lit cell steered with the D-pad in cell coordinates, erasing the cell it leaves and painting the one it enters so only two cells change per move and no trail is left.

nodes.name: GridCursor
nodes.summary: Module holding the cell size and board dimensions and the `RubyGBA.game` block that moves the cursor with `clear_cell`/`set_cell`, plus the `program` and `build_rom` delegators.

nodes.name: hero.rb
nodes.summary: Follow-camera showcase: a hero sprite walks a wrapping world larger than the screen via `camera_follows`, with mirrored facing art and a mist layer declared in front of the hero whose `transparency:` thickens as you walk north.
nodes.languageNotes: A background in front of a sprite is the one stacking order a picture cannot reach by accident, which is why `layers :ground, :actors, :air` has to be stated explicitly.

nodes.name: Hero
nodes.summary: Module holding the world tileset and map, the hero's mirrored walk poses, and the `RubyGBA.game` block wiring the follow camera and the variable-transparency mist layer, plus `program` and `build_rom`.

nodes.name: jukebox.rb
nodes.summary: The sound showcase: a three-tune music player where moving the menu cursor starts the highlighted classical piece, with a bobbing block row as a visible playing indicator. All melodies are written with the note/tempo `song` DSL.

nodes.name: Jukebox
nodes.summary: Module holding the screen layout constants, three `song` definitions and the `RubyGBA.game` block whose menu plays whichever row the cursor sits on, plus the `program` and `build_rom` delegators.

nodes.name: lake.rb
nodes.summary: Per-row scrolling showcase: `scroll_each_row` reads a sine table shifted each frame to roll a wave down a lake layer, over a fixed scenery layer and under a half-transparent layer of drifting jellyfish.
nodes.languageNotes: The row offsets are worked out in the gap between frames and handed to a DMA engine, so the water and the sprites floating on it always show the same frame; a fourth bending layer would fall back to per-scanline interrupts.

nodes.name: Lake
nodes.summary: Module holding the scenery, water and jellyfish tilesets and maps plus the sine table, and the `RubyGBA.game` block that bends the water layer per row each frame.

nodes.name: level.rb
nodes.summary: Map-import demo: imports a whole tile sheet as numbered tiles and reads a map-editor CSV export straight into a `background`, then walks an imported animated hero around it with `blocked_by` wall collision.

nodes.name: Level
nodes.summary: Module naming the tile sheet, hero sheet and CSV map paths and holding the `RubyGBA.game` block that imports them and steers the hero, plus the `program` and `build_rom` delegators.

nodes.name: maze.rb
nodes.summary: Tile-collision demo: a hero walks corridors it cannot leave, using `solid:` on the tileset plus `blocked_by` so the framework stops the sprite at walls and slides it along them with no collision code in the game.

nodes.name: Maze
nodes.summary: Module holding the maze tileset and map and the `RubyGBA.game` block that marks walls solid and blocks the hero against them, plus the `program` and `build_rom` delegators.

nodes.name: pacman.rb
nodes.summary: The tiled-mode flagship showcase: a tiled room, hardware sprites for Pac, pellets and a chasing ghost, per-direction `facing:` poses generated from a disc-and-mouth formula, sprite-vs-sprite collision and sound effects.

nodes.name: Pacman
nodes.summary: Module holding Pac's size and direction constants, the generated pose art, and the `RubyGBA.game` block with the room, pellets, ghost chase and scoring; its `DIRS`/`SIZE` constants and art formula are also reused by the sprite-sheet generator.

nodes.name: self.pacman_art
nodes.summary: Generates one Pac-Man pose as ASCII art: a yellow disc with a wedge bitten out on the side he faces, used for both the open- and shut-mouth frame of each direction.

nodes.name: parallax.rb
nodes.summary: Parallax demo: two stacked tile backgrounds — far sky with drifting clouds, near ground with trees — named by a `layers` declaration and scrolled at different speeds so the gap reads as depth.

nodes.name: Parallax
nodes.summary: Module holding the two tilesets and maps and the `RubyGBA.game` block that declares the layer stack and scrolls the near layer twice as fast as the far one, plus the `program` and `build_rom` delegators.

nodes.name: piano.rb
nodes.summary: Sampled-audio showcase: two animated hardware-sprite hands play a melody and block chords over a keyboard background, with every note re-pitched from one recorded piano sample by `instrument` and summed by the software mixer.

nodes.name: Piano
nodes.summary: Module holding the keyboard layout, the tune's notes and the imported hand art and WAV sample, and the `RubyGBA.game` block that animates the hands in step with the notes it triggers.

nodes.name: pixels.rb
nodes.summary: The smallest runnable example: a bitmap screen with no game loop, demonstrating `screen :bitmap`, `fill_rect`, `pixel` and `rgb`/named colors by drawing an Italian flag and three rows of RGB dots.

nodes.name: pong.rb
nodes.summary: Single-player Pong showing a large slice of the DSL at once: a `menu` title running on `screen :rotozoom` (per-scene display mode) with a row whose words change via `showing:`, `scene` + `case_var` state machine, `func` subroutines, `define_sound`/`beep` effects, a `song` for background music, `flash_screen :red` when the CPU scores, and `draw_text`/`draw_number` placed by name (`:center`, `within:`) rather than by counted pixels.

nodes.name: raycaster.rb
nodes.summary: A Wolfenstein-style first-person view of a grid maze, demonstrating `table` (a build-time sine curve and the maze itself shipped as ROM data), fractional numbers written as plain Floats for positions, steps and distances, and `draw_rect_at` drawing one wall column per screen strip at a height the game works out with the perspective divide.

nodes.name: Raycaster
nodes.summary: Namespace holding the maze constants, the precomputed sine and world tables, and the `RubyGBA.game` block that casts a ray per screen column each frame; exposes `program`/`build_rom` so tests can run the same program headlessly.

nodes.name: rotozoom_bg.rb
nodes.summary: Demonstrates `screen :rotozoom` and the background handle's `rotate`/`scale`: the D-pad turns and zooms a whole checkerboard layer about the middle of the screen, the effect a plain `screen :tiled` layer (which can only scroll) cannot do.

nodes.name: RotozoomBg
nodes.summary: Namespace holding the turn/zoom limits and the `RubyGBA.game` block that declares a checkerboard tileset on a rotozoom screen and eases its angle and scale from D-pad input.

nodes.name: scroll.rb
nodes.summary: Pans a camera over a world bigger than the screen: a 64x64-tile background (512x512 pixels, the largest a layer gets) moved with `scroll_by`/`scroll_to`, wrapping at its edge, with the framework laying the oversized map out across video memory unseen.

nodes.name: Scroll
nodes.summary: Namespace that generates the 64x64 grass/lake/tree map in plain Ruby at build time and holds the `RubyGBA.game` block whose loop scrolls the window from D-pad input.

nodes.name: sheet.rb
nodes.summary: Imports art from PNG files instead of ASCII art: `tiles from:` slices a tile sheet so each map character points at a cell, `sprite frames_from:` slices a walk cycle into animation frames, and `blocked_by` gives the hero tile collision against the room's solid tiles.

nodes.name: Sheet
nodes.summary: Namespace naming the two PNG assets and the 30x20 room map, holding the `RubyGBA.game` block that imports both sheets and steers a sheet-animated hero around the walls.

nodes.name: shmup.rb
nodes.summary: The worked example for splitting a game across files and for real scenes: `layers` names the stack once for parts declared in three different files, the ship/enemies/HUD are declared inside the `:playing` scene so they vanish on the game-over screen, and `fade_out under: :ui` dims the field while leaving the score readable.

nodes.name: Shmup
nodes.summary: Top-level namespace for the split-file shmup: holds the scene constants and the `RubyGBA.game` block that constructs the Player, Enemies and Hud collaborators inside the playing scene and wires the game-over transition.

nodes.name: enemies.rb
nodes.summary: The shmup's enemies as a spriteful `pool`: one declaration of fields and capacity, `spawn`/`each` instead of parallel arrays, and per-instance `facing:` + frame lists with `rate:` so each enemy flaps and leans toward the ship on its own schedule.

nodes.name: Enemies
nodes.summary: A plain Ruby collaborator taking the build and declaring the enemy pool and its art; `update` walks the live slots each frame to dive, face the ship, score a hit on the player's shot and cost a life on contact, with `respawn` returning a slot to the top at a random column.

nodes.name: hud.rb
nodes.summary: The shmup's heads-up display: tiled-mode `draw_text`/`draw_number` declared once (they repaint themselves from their variables every frame), placed with `:right`, `within:` and `text_width` so no column is a number counted by eye.

nodes.name: Hud
nodes.summary: Owns the score and lives variables and declares the on-screen bar inside the playing scene; exposes `score_up`, `hit` and `reset` so the other parts change the numbers without knowing how they are drawn.

nodes.name: player.rb
nodes.summary: The shmup's ship and its single shot, showing the collaborator pattern: a plain Ruby object that takes the build and calls `build.sprite`, `build.held`, `build.pressed` and `build.var` on it, using `move`/`clamp_to_screen` to steer and `above_top?` to reclaim the shot.

nodes.name: Player
nodes.summary: Declares the ship and shot sprites plus a live-shot flag; `update` steers and clamps the ship then runs `fire_when_ready` and `fly_the_shot`, with `reclaim_shot`/`reset` hiding the shot and returning the ship to its start.

nodes.name: snake.rb
nodes.summary: The classic Snake, showing `list` for the growing body, `grid` for cell-to-pixel coordinates, `every` for the movement beat, `save_var` for a high score that survives power-off, `seed`/`rand` for the food, and scenes wired with `case_var`; it deliberately repaints only the cells that changed, because a single-buffered screen cannot redraw the whole board inside the safe window.

nodes.name: Snake
nodes.summary: Namespace holding the board geometry constants and the `RubyGBA.game` block: title, playing and game-over scenes, the two body lists, the incremental board repaint, and the sound effects.

nodes.name: snake_buffered.rb
nodes.summary: The same Snake written the naive way — clear the screen and repaint walls, food, body and score every frame — to show what `screen :bitmap, tear_free: true` buys: the double-buffered screen never shows a half-drawn picture, so the obvious code is also the correct one.

nodes.name: BufferedSnake
nodes.summary: Namespace holding the board constants and the `RubyGBA.game` block for the tear-free variant, whose game loop repaints the whole field each pass instead of tracking which cells changed.

nodes.name: sparks.rb
nodes.summary: A particle shower that exists to show what `pool` is for: fixed slots with named fields, `spawn` once a frame at a random column, `each` walking the live ones, a spark removing itself off the bottom, plus `on_full: :recycle_oldest`, narrow field `widths:` and an `estimate:` hint for the cost report.

nodes.name: Sparks
nodes.summary: Namespace holding the slot count and the `RubyGBA.game` block whose loop clears the screen, spawns one spark and draws each live one as a two-pixel dot.

nodes.name: sprite_mover.rb
nodes.summary: Steers a hand-drawn heart around a bitmap screen to demonstrate the software `sprite` (it remembers the pixels under itself and repaints them, so it leaves no trail and the loop needs no `clear_screen`), and uses `layers`/`layer` to put one post in front of the heart and one behind it despite both being declared after it.

nodes.name: SpriteMover
nodes.summary: Namespace holding the screen and post geometry and the `RubyGBA.game` block that declares the three-deep layer stack, the heart sprite and the two posts, then moves the heart from D-pad input.

nodes.name: tiles.rb
nodes.summary: The worked example for tiled scenery: `image` tiles plus a `tiles` set plus a `background` map stamp a whole room, `set_tile` opens and shuts a door one cell at a time, and `show_map` swaps the entire background between three rooms — the way walking through a door works in a game with many rooms.

nodes.name: Tiles
nodes.summary: Namespace holding the four 8x8 tile images, the three room maps and the `RubyGBA.game` block that opens the door on A, shuts it on B, and walks between rooms with LEFT and RIGHT.

nodes.name: ruby_gba.rb
nodes.summary: The gem's entry point: it requires every part of the framework in dependency order and defines `RubyGBA.build`, the one call that turns a DSL block into a finished cartridge by evaluating the block into an IR tree, verifying it, running the guardrails, lowering it with `IR::Backends::GBA` and assembling the ROM.
nodes.languageNotes: A Ruby load-order barrel: ~60 `require_relative` lines precede the module body, so the require order encodes the framework's dependency order.

nodes.name: RubyGBA
nodes.summary: The top-level namespace and public build API: `ROMError`/`ProfileError`, the `build` pipeline, the measure-then-rebuild `build_measured`, and the warnings emitted when a scene cannot hold its frame rate or a saved profile names routines the program no longer has.

nodes.name: self.build
nodes.summary: The whole build pipeline in one call: evaluate the user's block into an IR program, check its internal consistency, run the guardrail checks (raising a friendly error on findings), lower it to ARM with the GBA backend, price the build-time findings, assemble the ROM and emit any requested disassembly.

nodes.name: self.build_measured
nodes.summary: Builds the game once, profiles every scene on the emulator, then builds it again knowing where its frames really went — so the choice of which routines live in the console's quick memory comes from measurement rather than from the shape of the program.

nodes.name: self.warn_of_slow_scenes
nodes.summary: Prints a plain-language warning naming each scene whose measured frames could not keep up, with the frame rate it actually produced.

nodes.name: self.warn_of_forgotten_routines
nodes.summary: Compares a saved profile against the routines the program actually defines and warns about names the measurement knows but the program no longer has — a stale profile deciding for code that is gone.

nodes.name: analyzer.rb
nodes.summary: Measures a built ROM's real per-frame cost on the emulator — the measured counterpart to the static estimate. Because a game costs what the player makes it cost, it holds each button the game reads in turn and then all at once, reads every frame over a window, and reports the worst frame it found and what was held to find it.

nodes.name: Analyzer
nodes.summary: Module-function API for measuring a program: per-scene profiling, button-combination attempts, worst/typical scanline readings, tearing detection, and a saturated path that instruments a frame counter to read a real frame rate once frames stop fitting.

nodes.name: profile
nodes.summary: Measures a program scene by scene: finds the scene dispatch, picks which scenes to measure, and boots a copy of the program straight into each one so the reading names the routines that scene really runs.

nodes.name: boot_into
nodes.summary: Copies the program and rewrites the scene selector's boot value, so a measurement starts and stays inside one scene instead of drifting out of it within a few frames.

nodes.name: measure_program
nodes.summary: Builds the program into a temporary ROM and runs one emulator attempt per button combination, keeping the worst reading and falling through to the saturated frame-rate measurement when a frame no longer fits.

nodes.name: attempt
nodes.summary: Runs one emulator probe over a window of frames with a given set of buttons held, returning the worst and typical scanline cost of those frames plus the worst tearing reading seen.

nodes.name: measure_saturated
nodes.summary: For a game whose frames overrun a whole frame's scanlines (where the scanline count stops being exact), instruments a frame counter into the program, runs it, and reports the real frame rate and per-pass work instead.

nodes.name: aseprite.rb
nodes.summary: Reads art the way pixel artists author it: parses an Aseprite JSON sprite-sheet export into plain data, and decodes the native binary `.aseprite` file directly — compositing layers, inflating the zlib cel data, resolving the palette, and keeping each frame's duration and the artist's named animations (frameTags).

nodes.name: Aseprite
nodes.summary: The Aseprite reader's namespace: the `Frame`/`Tag`/`Doc`/`FrameImage`/`Sprite` value objects, the JSON-export parser, and the entry point that loads a binary `.aseprite` file into decoded frames.

nodes.name: Decoder
nodes.summary: Walks the binary `.aseprite` container frame by frame and chunk by chunk, painting each visible layer's cel onto a canvas with its opacity, resolving pixels from the file's color depth and palette, and collecting the named animation tags.

nodes.name: parse
nodes.summary: Parses an Aseprite JSON export (both the array and hash frame layouts) into a `Doc` carrying the PNG it names, the frame rectangles with durations, and the named animations.

nodes.name: sprite
nodes.summary: Decodes the whole binary file into a `Sprite`: reads the header size and color depth, composites every frame's visible cels onto its own canvas, and returns those frames alongside the artist's animation tags.

nodes.name: paint_cel
nodes.summary: Reads one frame's chunks, keeping layer definitions and tags, and paints each cel chunk onto the frame canvas at the layer's opacity — skipping layers the artist hid.

nodes.name: blit_cel
nodes.summary: Copies one cel's pixels onto the canvas at its offset, honoring transparency and blending partly opaque layers, so a multi-layer drawing arrives as a single flattened frame.

nodes.name: pixel_color
nodes.summary: Turns one pixel of the file — indexed, grayscale or RGBA, depending on the document's color depth — into a console color plus an alpha, resolving palette entries and the document's transparent index.

nodes.name: asm.rb
nodes.summary: Encodes ARM (ARMv4T) instructions as raw 32-bit little-endian words — the bottom of the stack, used by the GBA lowering backend and by the `entry` raw-instruction escape hatch. Only the subset the DSL needs is implemented, plus helpers that answer whether an encoded word clobbers a given register.
nodes.languageNotes: Each method returns a binary String of whole 4-byte instructions, so emitted code is just string concatenation; condition codes are plain constants rather than an abstraction.

nodes.name: ASM
nodes.summary: The instruction encoder itself: condition codes, branches and calls, data processing, shifts, multiplies, byte/halfword/word loads and stores, push/pop, conditional forms, and the register-interference predicates the lowering pass consults.

nodes.name: disturbs?
nodes.summary: Answers whether one already-encoded instruction word writes to a given register — the check that lets the lowering pass know when a value it is holding in a scratch register has been clobbered.

nodes.name: data_processing_disturbs?
nodes.summary: The data-processing half of the interference check: decodes the opcode field to tell a real write apart from a compare or test, which set flags but leave their destination register alone.

nodes.name: encode_rotated_immediate
nodes.summary: Fits a constant into ARM's 8-bit-value-plus-even-rotation immediate field, returning nil when the value cannot be expressed that way so the caller falls back to loading it from memory.

nodes.name: author_source.rb
nodes.summary: Finds the first stack frame outside the framework so a diagnostic names the line the person actually wrote instead of the library file that raised it — turning `value.rb:388` into `hero.rb:42`.

nodes.name: AuthorSource
nodes.summary: Two module functions: `author_source` returns "file.rb:12" for the first frame outside lib/, and `at_author_line` formats it as a phrase to hang on the end of an error message (empty when every frame is the framework's own).

nodes.name: background.rb
nodes.summary: The handle the `background` verb hands back: scroll the visible window over a wrapping map, change one cell with `set_tile`, swap whole maps with `show_map`, bend the picture row by row with `scroll_each_row`, or turn and resize the layer with `rotate`/`scale` on a rotozoom screen — with friendly errors for the combinations the hardware cannot give.

nodes.name: Background
nodes.summary: Tracks a background's hidden scroll and map-selection variables and records IR nodes for every operation on it, exposing cells/rows, its solid-tile lookup for collision, and the affine angle and scale for a rotozoom layer.

nodes.name: set_tile
nodes.summary: Changes one cell of the map while the game runs, naming the tile the same way the map did; a cell outside the map is left alone, so a coordinate that ran off the edge needs no test around it.

nodes.name: show_map
nodes.summary: Swaps the whole background to another of its declared maps — by name or by a number the game works out — copying it in at the frame boundary and only when the answer changed.

nodes.name: scroll_to
nodes.summary: Puts the visible window at an absolute pixel position over the map, recording the move into the hidden scroll variables the framework applies once a frame.

nodes.name: scroll_each_row
nodes.summary: Gives every screen row its own sideways offset by running the author's block once per row in the gap between frames, so the layer bends — rippling water, heat haze, a melting transition — instead of moving as one flat rectangle.

nodes.name: rotate
nodes.summary: Turns the whole background to a heading in degrees, pivoting on the middle of the screen; refuses with a friendly error on a layer that only scrolls, and wraps the angle so 370 means 10.

nodes.name: scale
nodes.summary: Resizes the whole background about the middle of the screen, or with no argument hands the current size back as a `Value` so it can be eased with the ordinary expression DSL.

nodes.name: bounds.rb
nodes.summary: The rectangle-bounds contract for collision: anything that can answer `left`/`top`/`right`/`bottom` mixes this in and gains `overlaps?` plus the screen-edge tests (`off_screen?`, `off_left?`, `above_top?` and friends), each returning a `Condition` to branch on.

nodes.name: Bounds
nodes.summary: A mixin composing the four edges into comparisons: an inclusive rectangle overlap test and the has-it-left-the-screen questions, written so game code needs no coordinate literals or sprite-size arithmetic.

nodes.name: box.rb
nodes.summary: A rectangle in screen space made by the `box` verb: a corner and a size whose coordinates may each be a literal, a variable or an expression, so one box can describe a moving thing as naturally as a fixed wall. It draws nothing and exists to be collided against.

nodes.name: Box
nodes.summary: Coerces its four operands into `Value`s, aliases `left`/`top` to its corner and computes `right`/`bottom` as expressions, and mixes in `Bounds` so it gains `overlaps?` and the screen-edge tests for free.

nodes.name: branch.rb
nodes.summary: The open `if` that a `.then` just recorded, waiting for an optional `.else` to fill in what runs when the condition was false.

nodes.name: Branch
nodes.summary: Holds the builder and the if-node a `.then` produced; `else` records the false-side statements into that node, raising a friendly ArgumentError when the block is missing.

nodes.name: build_record.rb
nodes.summary: What the build worked out about a cartridge and the finished bytes cannot tell you afterwards — which routines were kept in quick memory, where each variable landed, which loops held their counter in a register, what each node emitted, and the guardrail findings — gathered into one value object so a ROM either carries a full report or carries none.

nodes.name: BuildRecord
nodes.summary: A `Data`-backed record of the source program, code placement, variable addresses, loop shapes, emitted counts, findings and the options the build was given; `fast_frame?` answers whether the per-frame routine made it into quick memory.
nodes.languageNotes: Subclasses `Data.define` and overrides `initialize` to supply defaults, keeping the record immutable while letting most fields be optional.

nodes.name: build_report.rb
nodes.summary: Renders the build-time half of `rom.profile`: routine sizes, which routines fit the console's 32K quick memory and which missed, the layer stack, video-memory usage and glyph counts. Every number is a fact the finished build already knows, never a model or prediction.
nodes.languageNotes: A `module_function` module rather than a class — the report is a pure rendering pass over an already-built ROM, so it holds no state.

nodes.name: BuildReport
nodes.summary: Module of `module_function` reporters that print what the build made of a program. Deliberately carries no claim about frame time — that is measured by running the game and printed by the Profiler underneath this report.

nodes.name: render
nodes.summary: Top-level entry point that prints every section of the build report in order: layer stack, video memory, quick memory, roomy memory, glyphs, column stretches and tearing.

nodes.name: stack_lines
nodes.summary: Prints the declared layer stack: each layer, what it holds, which of the console's four hardware priority levels it landed on, and how many levels remain.

nodes.name: transparency_line
nodes.summary: Reports the game's one see-through layer — that the display blends it for free, and, when the game also fades, that the fade borrows that blend while it runs.

nodes.name: video_memory_lines
nodes.summary: Reports how much of the console's picture memory the sprite art and background tiles took, and how much of the room left over came from storing small-palette pictures at half size.

nodes.name: quick_memory_lines
nodes.summary: Lists which routines the build placed in the console's 32K of quick memory, how big each came out, and how much of the budget is left — the roughly 2.3x speed difference nothing in a running ROM can report afterwards.

nodes.name: passed_over_lines
nodes.summary: Names the routines that missed quick memory, worst first, with what each one wanted and what was left when its turn came — the number a game cannot recover after the build.

nodes.name: as_json
nodes.summary: Returns the same build facts as a plain data structure instead of printed lines, so two builds can be compared programmatically.

nodes.name: builder.rb
nodes.summary: The DSL entry point. `Builder` requires and mixes in 18 concern modules to form the flat verb surface, and owns the shared build state — variable allocation, deferred function bodies, per-frame routines — plus the end-of-build finalization passes that turn deferred declarations into IR.
nodes.languageNotes: The flat DSL surface is kept while splitting the code by area: each concern is a module `include`d into one class, so every verb stays a top-level method on the build block's receiver.

nodes.name: Builder
nodes.summary: The DSL context a `RubyGBA.build` block is evaluated against. Every verb builds a node in an IR op-tree and returns; nothing emits machine code here. Building the whole tree before lowering any of it is what lets a `call` refer to a `func` defined later in the block.

nodes.name: EntryContext
nodes.summary: The receiver for an `entry` block — the raw-instruction escape hatch, exposing primitives like `loop_forever` and `nop` for what the DSL cannot express.

nodes.name: initialize
nodes.summary: Sets up the whole build state: frame-sync mode (:auto paces each game_loop, :manual leaves `wait_vblank` to the author), the IR root, and the dozens of registries for variables, functions, sprites, layers, backgrounds and per-frame routines.

nodes.name: list
nodes.summary: The `list` DSL verb: declares a runtime-sized collection with a capacity, an optional slot width (:byte/:half/:word), a fraction hint via `holds:`, a `fast:` memory placement override and a usual-length estimate.

nodes.name: table
nodes.summary: The `table` DSL verb: ships a build-time Ruby array as read-only ROM data, inferring signedness from the values and checking each one fits the chosen element width.

nodes.name: emit_pending_functions
nodes.summary: The finalization pass run once after the DSL block: drains and builds every deferred function body (draining rather than iterating, since building one body can declare another routine), scoping each scene's declarations to its own state gate and display mode, then runs every finalize/verify pass.

nodes.name: record_conditional
nodes.summary: Records a conditional IR node and its block, carrying the author's `estimate:` hint (how often the body usually runs) alongside the branch.

nodes.name: finalize_present_lists
nodes.summary: Fills each frame's present-objects node with the complete object list once all scenes are built, arranged in declared-layer order — the single place a frame's drawing order is settled, so no backend works it out for itself. A frame with no objects drops the node entirely.

nodes.name: finalize_background_scrolls
nodes.summary: Moves background scroll writes from where the author called them to the frame boundary, so scrolling can never tear. Which backgrounds scroll is only known now, because a scene's body is built after the loop that dispatches to it.

nodes.name: finalize_background_maps
nodes.summary: Places the map-swap copy for a multi-map background at the frame boundary, so `show_map` can be written anywhere and the whole room is copied in the gap between frames rather than mid-picture.

nodes.name: finalize_layer_blend
nodes.summary: Settles the display's single blend unit at the frame boundary — a see-through layer's amount, and the screen fade that borrows that blend while it runs.

nodes.name: finalize_per_frame_routines
nodes.summary: Inserts the `once_a_frame` routine calls just after each frame boundary, wrapped in a repeat over how many frames really passed — which is what makes those bodies keep real time on a game too heavy for one frame.

nodes.name: resolve_asset_path
nodes.summary: Resolves an asset filename (a PNG, a .wav, a CSV tilemap, an .aseprite file) relative to the author's own script rather than the process working directory, so a game folder is self-contained.

nodes.name: push_container
nodes.summary: Makes a node the current IR container for the duration of a block, so verbs called inside attach as its children — the mechanism behind `func`, `scene`, `game_loop`, `repeat` and every other block-taking verb.

nodes.name: collision.rb
nodes.summary: The collision concern of the DSL: the `box` verb for a plain test rectangle, and the shared tile-collision routine that lets a sprite or pool be `blocked_by` a tiled background — one routine for the whole program rather than a copy per mover.

nodes.name: Collision
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying collision verbs. Its tile check asks the map whether the cell a mover steps into is solid, so cost does not depend on how much the room is made of.

nodes.name: box
nodes.summary: The `box` DSL verb: makes a Box handle — a rectangle to test with `overlaps?` and the screen-edge tests — that draws nothing. Coordinates may be literals, variables or expressions.

nodes.name: build_tile_collision
nodes.summary: Builds the shared routine that tests a mover's hitbox against the solid cells of a tilemap, checking only the cells the box can touch so a second mover costs a call rather than another copy.

nodes.name: composition.rb
nodes.summary: The `pool` concern: many instances of a thing with named fields (bullets, enemies, particles) backed by parallel lists plus an active column, so the fields can never desync. Handles per-field slot widths, spawn-when-full policy, and pooled sprite art that faces and animates per instance.

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying the `pool` verb and all its build-time validation — capacity, field widths, pose sources and spawn-when-full policy.

nodes.name: PoolArt
nodes.summary: Immutable value object describing what a pool's instances look like — every picture flattened, the direction-to-row map, frames per direction, the animation rate and the shared collision box. Nil for a pure-data pool.
nodes.languageNotes: A `Data.define` with endless-method predicates — the project's preferred shape for an immutable value object over Struct.

nodes.name: pool
nodes.summary: The `pool` DSL verb: declares a capacity-bounded set of instances with named default-valued fields, optional sprite art, per-field slot widths and an on-full policy, returning a Pool handle with spawn/each/count.

nodes.name: pool_art!
nodes.summary: Resolves a pool's pose source — a single `image:`, directional `facing:` poses or a `frames:` flipbook — into a PoolArt, refusing two sources at once and requiring x/y fields for a spriteful pool.

nodes.name: validate_pool!
nodes.summary: Build-time guardrail for a pool declaration: checks the name, a positive capacity and well-formed field defaults, raising friendly plain-language errors rather than letting a malformed pool reach lowering.

nodes.name: setup_pool_storage
nodes.summary: Allocates the pool's backing storage: one list per field at its declared width, the byte-wide live column, and the free-slot stack sized to the largest slot number — all moved together by the pool's `fast:` placement.

nodes.name: setup_pool_art
nodes.summary: Gives a spriteful pool one hardware sprite object per slot, hidden until spawned, so each live instance composites at its own x/y.

nodes.name: control_flow.rb
nodes.summary: The control-flow concern: `game_loop`, `repeat`, `every`, `after`, `once_a_frame`, `wait_vblank`, `halt`, and the frame-boundary emitter that repaints sprites and HUD and advances animations once per pass — so a game author never writes a frame sync.

nodes.name: ControlFlow
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying every looping, timing and halting verb, plus the low-level `if_eq`/`if_ne`/`if_gt` family the expression DSL sits above.

nodes.name: game_loop
nodes.summary: The `game_loop` DSL verb: runs its body once per frame, with the framework placing the frame sync and the per-frame repaint at the top of every pass unless the build asked for :manual frame sync.

nodes.name: wait_vblank
nodes.summary: The `wait_vblank` DSL verb: waits for the safe window to draw and marks a frame boundary, which the finalization passes later use to place scroll writes, map swaps, blend changes and per-frame routines.

nodes.name: emit_frame_boundary
nodes.summary: Emits everything the framework does in the gap between frames: the vblank wait, the present-objects node that repaints sprites and HUD, and the animation advances — the machinery a game author never writes.

nodes.name: repeat
nodes.summary: The `repeat` DSL verb: a runtime-counted loop whose count may be a literal, a variable or a list length, with an optional `stop_when:` that turns the count into a ceiling and an `estimate:` documenting how many passes it usually makes.

nodes.name: every
nodes.summary: The `every` DSL verb: runs a body on a beat, counted in frames or seconds, using a hidden counter variable the author never declares.

nodes.name: once_a_frame
nodes.summary: The `once_a_frame` DSL verb: registers a routine that runs in the frame gap for each frame that really passed, so movement and effects keep real time even when a game is too heavy for one frame. The home for effects set off once and carried along afterwards.

nodes.name: timer_counter!
nodes.summary: Allocates and drives the hidden counter variable behind `every` and `after`, converting the requested interval to frames and rejecting a malformed one with a friendly error.

nodes.name: advance_animation
nodes.summary: Steps a registered sprite animation once per frame boundary: bumps the hidden rate counter and, on a step frame, advances the pose variable and wraps it at the cycle length.

nodes.name: debug.rb
nodes.summary: Debug and test-only build verbs, deliberately NOT part of the public game DSL and not mixed into Builder by default — a test or measurement harness opts in with `builder.extend(Builder::Debug)`.
nodes.languageNotes: Opting in via `extend` rather than `include` keeps these verbs off every game's build context while still routing them through the IR.

nodes.name: Debug
nodes.summary: Opt-in module of probing verbs. Its point is that even the project's own probing builds ordinary IR nodes rather than shipping raw assembly, so a debug program stays inspectable and is lowered by the real backend.

nodes.name: read_scanline
nodes.summary: Returns the scanline the console is drawing right now (0..227) as a Value, so a probe can measure how far into a frame the drawing has reached. Hardware-only — the headless reference interpreter refuses it.

nodes.name: drawing.rb
nodes.summary: The bitmap-drawing concern: `screen` mode selection, `pixel`, `fill_rect`, `clear_screen`, `dma_fill_rect`, the runtime-sized `draw_rect_at` and `draw_column_at`, plus the whole-screen effects `camera`, `fade` and `tint` and the `inside` clipping region.

nodes.name: Drawing
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying every direct-drawing verb and the screen-wide effects. Hides the display mode, VRAM layout and DMA behind plain intent and color names.

nodes.name: screen
nodes.summary: The `screen` DSL verb: picks the display kind (:bitmap, :tiled or :rotozoom), optional double buffering via `tear_free:`, and an explicit `colors:` table for art that already decided its palette order. Decides which kind of sprite and text the other verbs make.

nodes.name: inside
nodes.summary: The `inside` DSL verb: clips everything its block draws to a rectangle, so pixels outside are never worked out rather than being drawn and covered. Edges are settled at build time and regions do not nest — both friendly errors.

nodes.name: fade
nodes.summary: The `fade` DSL verb: fades the whole screen toward black or white by an amount 0..100, with an optional `under:` layer placing the fade in the stack so that layer and everything in front of it stay untouched.

nodes.name: tint
nodes.summary: The `tint` DSL verb: tints the whole screen toward any color by an amount 0..100 — free on a bitmap screen, and on a palette-driven screen done by blending the color table only on frames where the amount actually changed.

nodes.name: draw_column_at
nodes.summary: The `draw_column_at` DSL verb: draws one column of a picture stretched to a runtime height — the building block of a first-person view. Slice, x, top and height are all runtime values; a see-through picture costs only the rows that hold pixels.

nodes.name: draw_rect_at
nodes.summary: The `draw_rect_at` DSL verb: a rectangle whose position and size the game can all work out at runtime, any width including odd. A width or height of 0 or less draws nothing, so a bar can empty without a test around it.

nodes.name: given_colors
nodes.summary: Validates and records an explicit `colors:` palette for a tear-free screen: the order is preserved exactly, repeats kept, and `colors:` without `tear_free:` or two screens with different lists are friendly errors.

nodes.name: images.rb
nodes.summary: The image concern: declaring pictures from ASCII art, raw pixel data or PNG files, drawing them with `blit` (including one-of-a-set by a runtime value), reflecting them with `mirror`, and the color constructors `rgb`, `rgb8` and `color`.

nodes.name: Images
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying picture declaration and drawing. Builds palettes silently from the color names the author wrote, so a user never writes a slot number.

nodes.name: image
nodes.summary: The `image` DSL verb: declares a picture from ASCII art with a character-to-color map, from explicit width/height/data, or from a PNG file resolved next to the author's script.

nodes.name: blit
nodes.summary: The `blit` DSL verb: draws a named image at a runtime position, clipping at the screen edges, or one of a set of same-size pictures chosen by a runtime value via `showing:`.

nodes.name: blit_one_of
nodes.summary: Emits the picture-per-value form of `blit`: one test per picture, with a value outside the set drawing nothing so a still-settling number leaves the screen alone rather than drawing the wrong picture.

nodes.name: mirror
nodes.summary: The `mirror` DSL verb: returns the same picture facing the other way as a picture name usable anywhere a name goes, taking a list and returning a list so a whole direction's frames turn round in one word.

nodes.name: define_ascii_image
nodes.summary: Turns a block of ASCII art plus a character-to-color map into a pixel grid, checking every character is mapped and every row is the same width.

nodes.name: own_colors
nodes.summary: Applies an explicit `colors:` palette to one picture — the see-through entry first, at most sixteen entries — and raises a friendly error at the author's line for a pixel drawn in an unlisted color or one sitting on the transparent entry.

nodes.name: record_visible_bounds
nodes.summary: Records the box hugging a picture's non-transparent pixels — the default collision box for a sprite and the cheap gate in front of per-pixel collision.

nodes.name: input.rb
nodes.summary: The input concern: `held` (1 while a button is down) and `pressed` (1 on the press edge only) as expression values, plus the low-level `if_held`/`if_pressed` block forms and the guardrail that rejects an unknown button by name.

nodes.name: Input
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying button reads. An unknown button name is a friendly error rather than a silently dead test.

nodes.name: held
nodes.summary: The `held` DSL verb: a Value that is 1 while the named button is down, for continuous actions like walking.

nodes.name: pressed
nodes.summary: The `pressed` DSL verb: a Value that is 1 only on the frame a button goes down, so holding it fires once — the reason a trigger belongs in the game loop rather than a per-frame routine.

nodes.name: layers.rb
nodes.summary: The layer concern: `layers` declares the back-to-front stack once, `layer` puts declarations at a named depth, with optional `transparency:`. Most of the file is guardrails — refusing a scene inside a layer, a painting verb inside one, a declaration deferred into a routine, a second see-through layer, or a stack needing more than the console's four depth levels.

nodes.name: Layers
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder giving depth a name. A layer holds things, not brushstrokes — so retained-mode declarations belong in one and immediate painting verbs are refused with a friendly error.

nodes.name: layers
nodes.summary: The `layers` DSL verb: declares the whole stack back to front, once and globally, because "in front of" is a relation across the whole screen. A repeated name or a second declaration is a friendly error.

nodes.name: layer
nodes.summary: The `layer` DSL verb: runs a block with a named depth in force, so backgrounds, sprites, spriteful pools and tiled text declared inside belong to that layer. `transparency:` makes it see-through, by a fixed amount or one the game works out.

nodes.name: place_in_layer
nodes.summary: Tags a freshly declared node with the layer currently in force, leaving anything declared outside a layer exactly where it was so adopting layers piecemeal can never move an untagged thing.

nodes.name: verify_stack_fits!
nodes.summary: End-of-build check that the declared stack fits the console's four depth levels — a level is spent only by a background, so many sprite layers can share one. Names the layer that cost the level and shows the stack when it does not fit.

nodes.name: check_one_transparent_layer!
nodes.summary: Refuses a second see-through layer, naming the one the game already has — a transparent layer sitting directly over another is the one arrangement the two backends would draw differently.

nodes.name: refuse_painting_in_layer!
nodes.summary: Rejects immediate painting verbs inside a layer block — a layer holds things, not brushstrokes, and no ordering applied later could reach back and move pixels already painted into the framebuffer.

nodes.name: check_effect_layer!
nodes.summary: Validates the `under:` layer a screen effect names: the layer must be declared, the screen must be tiled, and a game gets one fade at one depth — a second depth, or a colored fade placed at all, is a friendly error.

nodes.name: refuse_deferred_layer!
nodes.summary: Rejects declaring a sprite or background inside a routine written in a layer block: the body is built later, when the layer is not in force, so it would quietly sit at no depth at all. The error names what was written and the way round that works.

nodes.name: music.rb
nodes.summary: The music concern: `song` declares a tune from notes, rests, tempo and up to two layered voices; `play_song` starts one and `stop_music` silences both music voices.

nodes.name: Music
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying the music verbs. The framework picks which sound channels a song's voices use, so an author writes a melody over a bass line and never names a channel.

nodes.name: song
nodes.summary: The `song` DSL verb: evaluates a block in a SongContext where `tempo`, `note`, `rest`, `duty`, `volume` and `voice` build the tune, and registers the finished song under its name.

nodes.name: randomness.rb
nodes.summary: The randomness concern: `seed` and `randomize` set up the pseudo-random stream, `roll` stores a random value in a variable, `rand` returns one as an expression, and `chance` gives a percentage-true Condition.

nodes.name: Randomness
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying random values. It allocates and churns the RNG state variables itself, so an author never declares a seed variable or writes the generator.

nodes.name: roll
nodes.summary: The `roll` DSL verb: churns the RNG and stores a value from the given range in a named variable, reducing the raw stream onto the range's width.

nodes.name: chance
nodes.summary: The `chance` DSL verb: returns a Condition that holds the given percentage of the time, for `.then { }` — a random roll and a comparison in one word.

nodes.name: range_bounds
nodes.summary: Normalizes a Ruby Range (inclusive or exclusive) into a low bound and width, rejecting an empty, reversed or out-of-32-bit-range one with a friendly error.

nodes.name: sampled_audio.rb
nodes.summary: The sampled-audio concern: `sample` loads a recorded 8-bit PCM clip from a .wav file or raw array, and `instrument` wraps the same clip as something you play notes on. The FIFO, DMA, timer and software mixer stay hidden behind the handle.

nodes.name: SampledAudio
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying recorded sound. Several samples can play at once through a software mixer; a ninth voice is dropped rather than stealing one.

nodes.name: sample
nodes.summary: The `sample` DSL verb: declares a recorded clip from a .wav file resolved next to the author's script, or from raw PCM at a given rate, tagged with the note it was recorded at so it can be pitch-shifted later.

nodes.name: pack_pcm
nodes.summary: Packs raw sample data into the signed 8-bit byte string the hardware reads, accepting either an Array of -128..127 values or an already-packed String and rejecting anything else with a friendly error.

nodes.name: scenes.rb
nodes.summary: The subroutine and game-state concern: `func`/`call` for a routine emitted once and called many times, `scene` for a named game state, `case_var` with `when_val` to run exactly one scene per frame, and the end-of-build check that every call and case target exists.

nodes.name: Scenes
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying routines and game states. A scene owns what it declares — its sprites and HUD show only while it is the active state — which is also what makes the video-memory budget one scene's rather than the whole game's.

nodes.name: CaseContext
nodes.summary: The receiver for a `case_var` block, collecting `when_val value, :scene_name` pairs that become the per-frame dispatch from a state variable to exactly one scene.

nodes.name: func
nodes.summary: The `func` DSL verb: declares a subroutine whose body is deferred until the end of the build, so a `call` can name a func defined later. `fast:` overrides the framework's choice of whether it lives in the console's quick memory.

nodes.name: scene
nodes.summary: The `scene` DSL verb: declares a named game state as a deferred routine run once per frame while active, with everything declared inside belonging to that scene.

nodes.name: case_var
nodes.summary: The `case_var` DSL verb: dispatches on a state variable to run exactly one scene per frame, reloading the variable before each comparison since a scene call clobbers the scratch register.

nodes.name: verify_targets_defined!
nodes.summary: End-of-build check that every `call` and every `when_val` names a routine that actually exists, turning a misspelled scene name into a friendly error instead of a silent jump to nowhere.

nodes.name: sound.rb
nodes.summary: The synthesized-sound concern: `enable_sound`, `define_sound`/`beep` for square-wave effects on channel 2, `noise` for percussion and explosions on the noise voice, and `wave`/`stop_wave` for a sustained richer tone on the wave voice.

nodes.name: Sound
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying the console's synthesized voices. Effects use channel 2 and music channel 1, so a beep never cuts off the tune.

nodes.name: beep
nodes.summary: The `beep` DSL verb: plays a named or ad-hoc square-wave tone on the effects channel, with optional duty, decay and volume overrides.

nodes.name: note_frequency
nodes.summary: Turns a pitch given as a note name (:C4, :E4) or a raw Hz number into the frequency value the sound hardware wants, so an author writes notes rather than register numbers.

nodes.name: sprite_import.rb
nodes.summary: Sprite art adapters that feed the sprite builder: slicing a flipbook out of a sheet (`frames_from:`), slicing a four-way character's rows and columns (`facing_from:`), and reading a native .aseprite file or its JSON export into named animations.

nodes.name: SpriteImport
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder turning external art files into the poses a `sprite` wants, so an author never names or numbers individual frames.

nodes.name: import_frames
nodes.summary: Slices a sprite sheet into equal-size frames for `frames_from:`, defining one image per cell and returning them in order as a flipbook cycle.

nodes.name: import_facing
nodes.summary: Slices a directional sheet for `facing_from:` — each row a direction in `dirs:` order, each column a frame of that direction — producing either a still pose per direction or a per-direction animation.

nodes.name: import_aseprite
nodes.summary: Turns a loaded Aseprite document into the sprite's poses and named animations, exposing each frameTag as something `play(:walk)` can run and taking frame speed from the authored durations.

nodes.name: load_aseprite
nodes.summary: Reads the art file itself — the native .aseprite binary (compositing layers, decompressing frames, resolving the palette) or a JSON export whose frames are sliced from the PNG named in its meta.image.

nodes.name: sprites.rb
nodes.summary: The sprite concern: the one `sprite` verb that makes a software save-under sprite on a bitmap screen or a hardware OAM sprite on a tiled one, plus pose resolution for `facing:`/`frames:`/clip animations, hitbox derivation, and the rotate/scale attributes.

nodes.name: Sprites
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying sprites. The screen mode picks which kind gets made, so the same game code works on either — and a picture bigger than any hardware rectangle is cut up and kept together as one sprite.

nodes.name: sprite
nodes.summary: The `sprite` DSL verb: validates the pose source, resolves the art, derives the collision box and dispatches to the software or hardware sprite builder according to the current screen mode, returning a handle with move/face/overlaps? and the screen-edge tests.

nodes.name: hardware_sprite
nodes.summary: Builds the OAM-composited sprite for a tiled screen: allocates position and pose variables, uploads the poses, and cuts a picture larger than the console's biggest rectangle into pieces drawn together at one depth.

nodes.name: collision_box
nodes.summary: Derives a sprite's collision box from its `hitbox:` option — `:full` for the whole image, a number to inset each side, an explicit rectangle, or by default the union of the poses' visible-pixel bounds.

nodes.name: resolve_sprite_art
nodes.summary: Flattens a `facing:` hash or `frames:` list into the pose list, direction map, frames-per-direction and shared width/height that both a sprite and a pool are built from.

nodes.name: resolve_directional_frames
nodes.summary: Handles the per-direction animation form of `facing:` — a list of frames per direction — checking every direction has the same frame count and composing facing plus frame into one pose index.

nodes.name: validate_animation!
nodes.summary: Build-time guardrail for a sprite or pool's animation: `facing:` and `frames:` are mutually exclusive, a cycle needs a rate, and every pose must be the same size — each a friendly error naming what was written.

nodes.name: clip_sprite
nodes.summary: Builds the software (bitmap-screen) form of a sprite with named Aseprite-style clips, wiring each clip's frame range and durations so `play(:walk)` switches which cycle runs.

nodes.name: clip_hardware_sprite
nodes.summary: The tiled-screen counterpart of clip_sprite: an OAM sprite whose named clips select which uploaded pose the console draws.

nodes.name: setup_clip_animation
nodes.summary: Registers the per-frame machinery behind named clips: the hidden clip, frame and countdown variables advanced at each frame boundary, with the current clip looping until another is played.

nodes.name: text.rb
nodes.summary: The text concern: `font` defines a bitmap font from glyph art or supplied pictures; `draw_text` and `draw_number` place strings and live numbers, painting into the framebuffer on a bitmap screen or declaring per-character hardware glyph sprites on a tiled one. Also owns named alignment (:left/:center/:right) and `text_width`.

nodes.name: Text
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying text and numbers. The one verb family whose nature changes with the screen: immediate painting on bitmap, a once-declared redrawn-for-you HUD on tiled.

nodes.name: font
nodes.summary: The `font` DSL verb: defines a bitmap font either from a block of glyph art or from supplied per-character pixel rows via `glyphs:`, each glyph keeping its own width so a proportional alphabet stays proportional.

nodes.name: draw_text
nodes.summary: The `draw_text` DSL verb: draws a string at a column or a named alignment, optionally with a two-color pair chosen by a `showing:` test — which on a tiled screen becomes one recolored sprite per character instead of two.

nodes.name: draw_number
nodes.summary: The `draw_number` DSL verb: draws a live number right-aligned in a fixed-width digit field with no leading zeros, following its variable and updating itself. Places the field rather than the number, so a centered score does not jitter as it counts up.

nodes.name: text_colors!
nodes.summary: Validates the color argument against `showing:`: exactly two colors with a test, one without. Three colors, or a pair with no test, is a friendly error saying to draw the text under a test for each.

nodes.name: column_for
nodes.summary: Turns a column argument into a real pixel column — a number stays itself, while :left/:center/:right are placed against `within:`, the enclosing `inside` region, or the whole screen, using the font's own measured width.

nodes.name: draw_live_number
nodes.summary: Paints a runtime number into the framebuffer digit by digit: divides out each place into a scratch variable and draws one shared glyph routine per digit rather than re-emitting the shapes per place.

nodes.name: draw_text_tiled
nodes.summary: Declares a string as one 8x8 hardware glyph sprite per character on a tiled screen, riding any enclosing condition onto the glyphs so they show exactly while it holds.

nodes.name: draw_number_tiled
nodes.summary: Declares a live number as hardware glyph sprites whose poses follow the digit at each place, so the HUD figure updates itself every frame without being redrawn by the game.

nodes.name: glyph_image
nodes.summary: Makes (and caches) the picture for one character of a font in one color, so the same letter drawn twice in the same color costs one image.

nodes.name: fits_a_glyph_tile!
nodes.summary: Checks every character of a font fits the console's 8x8 glyph sprite on a tiled screen, naming the widest character in the friendly error when an imported alphabet is too big.

nodes.name: require_hud_declared_once!
nodes.summary: Enforces that tiled text is declared once — above the game loop or inside a scene — rather than loose inside the loop, and says which of the two places the author is in.

nodes.name: tiled.rb
nodes.summary: The tiled-graphics concern: `tiles` declares a tileset from named images or an imported sheet (with solid cells for collision), and `background` stamps a grid from an inline map, a CSV export or a hash of swappable maps — plus scrolling, per-row bending and the rotozoom affine mode.

nodes.name: Tiled
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying tile backgrounds. Picks the console's grid size, lays out a map too big for one piece of video memory and gives each layer its own tile-numbering base — none of which appears in the program.

nodes.name: tiles
nodes.summary: The `tiles` DSL verb: builds a tileset by mapping characters to tile images, to cells of an imported sheet, or by numbering a whole sheet for a CSV map, with `solid:` marking the cells a sprite cannot move through.

nodes.name: background
nodes.summary: The `background` DSL verb: stamps a grid of tiles from an inline map, a CSV file or a hash of several same-size maps the game can swap between, returning a handle with scroll_by/scroll_to, set_tile and show_map.

nodes.name: background_maps
nodes.summary: Resolves a background's `map:`/`from:` argument into one or several named tile grids, so a hash of rooms becomes the numbered maps `show_map` selects between at runtime.

nodes.name: make_background_affine
nodes.summary: Converts a background to the rotate/scale (rotozoom) form: allocates its angle and scale variables and registers the per-frame affine update, while making the plain scroll verbs a friendly error on it.

nodes.name: record_row_bend
nodes.summary: Registers `scroll_each_row`: runs the author's block once per screen row in the gap between frames, giving each row its own sideways offset so a layer ripples or melts instead of moving as one flat rectangle.

nodes.name: define_sheet_tileset
nodes.summary: Imports a whole tile sheet as numbered tiles (1, 2, 3… left to right — the numbering a map editor exports), honoring cut-out transparency and taking `solid:` as tile numbers.

nodes.name: csv_image_grid
nodes.summary: Turns a CSV tilemap file exported from a map editor into the grid of tile images a background stamps, with 0 meaning an empty cell.

nodes.name: parse_csv_tilemap
nodes.summary: Parses CSV tilemap text into rows of integers, rejecting a ragged grid or a non-numeric cell with a friendly error that names the file and the line.

nodes.name: merge_solid_cells
nodes.summary: Merges runs of adjacent solid cells into larger rectangles, so a wall drawn as dozens of tiles becomes a handful of collision rectangles.

nodes.name: timers.rb
nodes.summary: The hardware-timer concern: the `timer` verb declares a free-running counter ticking at a chosen rate, independent of the frame loop, returning a handle with `ticks`, `on_tick` and `stop`.

nodes.name: Timers
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying the `timer` verb — a low-level building block the higher-level `every`/`after` verbs sit above, for precise free-running timing rather than frame-paced gameplay.

nodes.name: timer
nodes.summary: The `timer` DSL verb: allocates a hardware counter at the requested ticks per second and returns a Timer handle. Sampled audio reserves one timer, so user timers allocate from timer 1 upward.

nodes.name: variables.rb
nodes.summary: The variable concern: `var` and `save_var` declare state (the latter surviving power-off in cartridge save memory), `set`/`copy`/`add`/`sub`/`negate`/`abs` mutate it, and `clamp` and `approach` cap or ease a value toward a target with bounds that may themselves be computed.

nodes.name: Variables
nodes.summary: Concern module mixed into Builder supplying named state. Variables live at fixed offsets in the console's quick memory — which is what makes a read two instructions instead of four, and why a program with too many is a friendly error suggesting a list.

nodes.name: var
nodes.summary: The `var` DSL verb: declares a variable and returns a Value handle. The initial value is applied once at boot, so declaring inside a scene or loop still initializes a single time.

nodes.name: save_var
nodes.summary: The `save_var` DSL verb: a variable kept in cartridge save memory that survives power-off — a high score, an unlock, a setting. Every change is mirrored out automatically, with no separate save step and no SRAM address at the surface.

nodes.name: clamp
nodes.summary: The `clamp` DSL verb: holds a variable between a minimum and maximum, either of which may be a literal or something the game works out at runtime.

nodes.name: approach
nodes.summary: The `approach` DSL verb: moves a variable toward a target by at most one step, capped so it never overshoots. A computed step is read as a distance, so a negative one still moves toward the target and zero holds still.

nodes.name: approach_bounds
nodes.summary: Works out the clamp bounds that stop `approach` overshooting — for a literal step at build time, and for a computed one as the absolute distance either side of the target.

nodes.name: fraction_node_for
nodes.summary: Detects a Float initial value and gives the variable a fixed-point scale, which every handle for it then carries so arithmetic keeps the fraction without the author ever writing "fixed point".

nodes.name: cli.rb
nodes.summary: The `ruby-gba` command-line interface, built on Thor: `build` compiles a game file to a .gba cartridge (or emits its IR), `profile` runs the finished ROM and reports where its frames went, `inspect` disassembles a ROM, and `new` scaffolds a starter game.
nodes.languageNotes: Thor is required here and in bin/ruby-gba only — never by the library — so building a ROM in code or in a test does not depend on it.

nodes.name: CLI
nodes.summary: Thor subclass defining every `ruby-gba` command with its options and long descriptions. Overrides `exit_on_failure?` to true, since without it Thor reports a failed command but still exits 0.

nodes.name: build
nodes.summary: The `build` command: dispatches on --format to emit either a .gba cartridge or a standalone Ruby class holding the game's IR, rejecting any other format by name.

nodes.name: profile
nodes.summary: The `profile` command: builds the game, then runs it and prints what the build made of it plus where its frames actually went, optionally holding buttons or pinning the game to one scene to reach the moment worth measuring.

nodes.name: new
nodes.summary: The `new` command: scaffolds a starter game file from a template so a first ROM is one command away.

nodes.name: build_cartridge
nodes.summary: Loads the game file, writes the .gba next to it (or to --output), and optionally prints the packing stats and the profile.

nodes.name: build_ir
nodes.summary: Emits the game's intermediate representation as a standalone Ruby class that reconstructs the IR and lowers it — paged to the terminal, or written to --output like the .gba would be.

nodes.name: load_game
nodes.summary: Requires the author's game file and returns the ROM its `RubyGBA.game` declaration produced, turning a missing file or a file that declares no game into a clear Thor error.

nodes.name: starter_source
nodes.summary: The template text for `ruby-gba new`: a small working game showing the shape of a build block, so a beginner starts from something that runs.

nodes.name: color.rb
nodes.summary: 15-bit BGR555 color handling: named presets, `rgb`/`rgb8` channel packing, `from_hex` for CSS-style strings, and `resolve` which turns whatever the author wrote — a name, a hex string, a raw value — into a color word.
nodes.languageNotes: The GBA packs color as 0bBBBBBGGGGGRRRRR — blue in the high bits, red in the low ones, five bits each — which is why an 8-bit value passed to `rgb` is rejected rather than silently truncated.

nodes.name: Color
nodes.summary: Module of color utilities and the PRESETS table of named colors, so a game author writes `:red` and never a 15-bit word.

nodes.name: rgb
nodes.summary: Packs three 0-31 channels into a 15-bit color, raising on an out-of-range channel to catch the common mistake of passing 8-bit values.

nodes.name: rgb8
nodes.summary: Packs three 0-255 channels into a 15-bit color by scaling each down to five bits, for anyone working from ordinary 8-bit color values.

nodes.name: from_hex
nodes.summary: Parses a CSS-style hex string ("#00FF00") into a 15-bit color, so art tooling and web palettes drop straight in.

nodes.name: resolve
nodes.summary: The single entry every drawing verb funnels its color argument through: a preset name, a hex string or an already-packed value all become one 15-bit word, with an unknown name raising a friendly error.

nodes.name: condition.rb
nodes.summary: The `Condition` handle — the result of comparing two Values. Branch with `.then`/`.else`, combine with `&` and `|`. Tracks itself in the builder's pending set at birth so a comparison dropped into a native Ruby `if` (which is truthy, and would emit its body unconditionally) is caught rather than silently miscompiled.
nodes.languageNotes: Ruby cannot overload `&&`/`||`, so the single-character `&` and `|` are the forms that build a combined Condition — and because any object is truthy, a native `if` on a Condition is the footgun the pending-set tracking exists to catch.

nodes.name: Condition
nodes.summary: A yes/no test the program branches on, wrapping a comparison IR node. Records where the author built it so the orphaned-condition diagnostic can point at their own line.

nodes.name: then
nodes.summary: Branches on the condition, recording the block as the body and taking it out of the builder's pending set. An `estimate:` hint says how often the body usually runs.

nodes.name: how_often
nodes.summary: Normalizes the `estimate:` hint on a branch into runs-per-period, defaulting an omitted period to one frame so `usually: 0` reads as "not on a normal frame".

nodes.name: compose
nodes.summary: Builds the combined Condition behind `&` and `|`, consuming both operands out of the pending set so only a genuinely unused comparison is reported.

nodes.name: constants.rb
nodes.summary: GBA hardware constants — the memory map, display registers, DMA channels, sound registers and their flag bits — named after the tonc/libgba conventions. Included into Builder so lowering code can name a register rather than an address.
nodes.languageNotes: The GBA memory map is flat: there is no OS and no filesystem, so every piece of hardware is reached as a fixed address — EWRAM at 0x02000000 (256KB, 16-bit bus) and the fast IWRAM at 0x03000000 (32KB, 32-bit bus).

nodes.name: Constants
nodes.summary: The one place a hardware address or flag bit is written down, grouped and commented by region so a reader learns what each piece of hardware is while looking it up.

nodes.name: direction.rb
nodes.summary: Names the four screen directions and their diagonals as [dx, dy] unit steps, so game code can say `move :left` instead of doing the arithmetic. Shared vocabulary for anything that moves or faces a way, not only sprites.

nodes.name: Direction
nodes.summary: Module holding the UNIT table — direction name to [dx, dy] step in screen coordinates, so `up` decreases y — plus the two lookups over it.

nodes.name: unit
nodes.summary: Returns the [dx, dy] unit step for a direction name, raising a friendly error that lists the known directions when the name is a typo.

nodes.name: effects.rb
nodes.summary: The effect registry: how a verb pack is added to the DSL. It holds the DEFAULT_PACKS that ship on (shake, fade, follow camera, pulse, menu, keep_showing), defines each pack's verbs onto the Builder, and enforces the rule that a pack may only compose public DSL verbs — new capability is kernel, new convenience is a pack.
nodes.languageNotes: Ruby metaprogramming: a shared VERBS module gains each pack's methods via define_method + instance_method, then is included into Builder, so a name clash is refused at registration rather than silently shadowing a verb.

nodes.name: Effects
nodes.summary: The registry singleton: registers single verbs and whole packs, claims names so nothing can shadow a Builder verb, forwards a pack's guardrail checks to IR::Guardrails, and can unregister everything non-default again for tests.

nodes.name: register_pack
nodes.summary: Registers a whole pack: claims every public verb and private helper name, defines them onto the shared VERBS module, and registers the pack's guardrail checks.

nodes.name: follow_camera.rb
nodes.summary: Effect pack for `camera_follows`: it keeps a sprite where it stands on screen and scrolls the background by whatever drift the game's own `move` produced, so a world bigger than the screen is written with ordinary sprite code.

nodes.name: FollowCamera
nodes.summary: The pack module: the `camera_follows` verb, the two hidden home-position variables, the per-frame follow routine, and the argument checks behind its friendly errors.
