nodes.summary: Turns an absolute tile address into the number a map cell holds, counted from whichever of the four fixed starting points that layer uses.

nodes.name: check_they_still_fit!
nodes.summary: Raises Full when the tile end and the map end have crossed, which is the moment the build must stop rather than ship a scrambled screen.

nodes.name: timers.rb
nodes.summary: Allocates and configures the console's four hardware timers: picks the finest prescaler and reload value for a requested rate, chains a cascade timer to count overflows for a readable tick count, and emits the register writes that start and stop them.
nodes.languageNotes: A timer whose overflow count is read costs a PAIR of hardware timers — the rate timer plus a cascade timer that ticks once per overflow — because the raw counter races too fast to read.

nodes.name: Timers
nodes.summary: Owns the hardware-timer allocation table, handing out timers in order and letting the audio mixer reserve one ahead of anything the program named.

nodes.name: register_timers
nodes.summary: Walks the program to find every timer it starts and whether each one's tick count is ever read, then registers them in declaration order.

nodes.name: register_timer
nodes.summary: Assigns one logical timer its hardware slot — a pair when its overflows are counted — and raises when the four run out.

nodes.name: emit_timer_start
nodes.summary: Emits the reload and control register writes that start a timer at its chosen prescaler, plus the cascade timer behind it when the count is read.

nodes.name: reference.rb
nodes.summary: The reference backend: runs an IR program directly in Ruby against simulated hardware — a fake screen, a fake gamepad, an in-memory variable store, timers and a voice mixer — so a program's logic and its visible pixels can be checked in-process with no ROM and no emulator.
nodes.languageNotes: The second independent answer the differential tests compare the real ROM against — an emulator alone cannot tell a faithful lowering of the wrong thing from the right thing.

nodes.name: Reference
nodes.summary: The interpreter itself: holds the variable store, framebuffer, lists, tables, objects, backgrounds, timers and audio voices, and walks the IR tree executing statements and evaluating expressions frame by frame.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: Entry point that collects the program's definitions then executes it, stopping at a frame budget or step budget so a test can never hang on a game loop.

nodes.name: collect_definitions
nodes.summary: Pre-walks the tree to register everything declared rather than executed — funcs, scenes, images, fonts, songs, samples, tables, layers and objects — before a single statement runs.

nodes.name: tick!
nodes.summary: Counts one step of execution against the budget and raises a clear error when a program has run away, naming what it was doing.

nodes.name: exec
nodes.summary: The central statement dispatcher: one giant case over every IR node kind, executing control flow, variable ops, drawing, audio, lists, sprites, layers and timers, and raising on a kind this backend does not support.

nodes.name: advance_frame
nodes.summary: Models the frame boundary: flips the pages, runs each timer's accrued handler calls, advances audio voices, applies the input script and repaints bent backgrounds.

nodes.name: start_sample
nodes.summary: Starts a sampled-audio voice, working out how many frames it will sound for from its length, rate and pitch shift, and tracking the peak voice count.

nodes.name: advance_voices
nodes.summary: Ages every sounding voice by one frame and retires the ones that have finished, mirroring how the real mixer refills once a frame.

nodes.name: exec_background
nodes.summary: Registers a tiled background with its tileset and one or more maps, and stamps it into the picture on a bitmap screen where a background is painted once.

nodes.name: exec_set_tile
nodes.summary: Changes one map cell to a different tile at run time, leaving a coordinate outside the map alone rather than raising — matching what the console does.

nodes.name: paint_background_window
nodes.summary: Paints the visible 240x160 window of a scrolling tiled layer, wrapping at the grid edge and applying any per-row bend offset as it walks each line.

nodes.name: paint_affine_background_window
nodes.summary: Paints a rotating and scaling background by walking screen pixels back through the transform matrix to find which map cell and tile pixel each one shows.

nodes.name: composite_scrolled_frame
nodes.summary: Builds one frame of a tiled screen by painting the backgrounds in stack order, then the sprite layers, honouring which layer is see-through and where a fade sits in the stack.

nodes.name: exec_present_objects
nodes.summary: Draws every active sprite for the frame in stack order, picking each one's current pose and applying its rotation or scale where it has one.

nodes.name: exec_draw_column_at
nodes.summary: Draws one column of a picture stretched to a run-time height — the first-person wall strip — clipping at the screen edges and skipping rows the picture leaves transparent.

nodes.name: blit_image_transformed
nodes.summary: Draws a picture rotated or resized about its own centre by sampling the source through the inverse transform, the interpreter's stand-in for the console's sprite rotate/scale hardware.

nodes.name: pixels_overlap?
nodes.summary: Per-pixel sprite collision: intersects the two bounding boxes first, then checks whether any pixel drawn by both poses actually meets.

nodes.name: eval_node
nodes.summary: Evaluates one expression node — a literal, a variable read, a binary operation, a list or table read, a button test, a timer count or a collision test — into a plain integer.

nodes.name: eval_binop
nodes.summary: Applies a binary operator through Int32 so the interpreter's arithmetic wraps, shifts and divides exactly the way the console's does.

nodes.name: framebuffer.rb
nodes.summary: A simulated screen for the reference backend: a 240x160 grid of colors that drops out-of-bounds writes silently, models the two-page tear-free screen, and applies camera offset, fade, tint and layer blending when a pixel is read back.
nodes.languageNotes: Reads distinguish the stored pixel from the shown pixel, so a test can assert either what the program drew or what a player would see through a fade.

nodes.name: Framebuffer
nodes.summary: The fake screen object: holds the pixel grid (one or two pages), the clip area, the camera offset, the fade and tint levels, and the blend state a see-through layer sets.

nodes.name: initialize
nodes.summary: Builds the pixel grid at the shared display contract's size and sets up the clip area, camera and blend state at their neutral values.

nodes.name: paged=
nodes.summary: Switches between one picture and two: the tear-free screen keeps a shown page and a drawn page that trade places at the frame boundary.

nodes.name: paint_row
nodes.summary: Writes a run of colors into one row in a single pass, the fast path the tile and background painters use.

nodes.name: fill_rect
nodes.summary: Fills a rectangle with one color, clipped to both the screen and any area an `inside` block is holding drawing to.

nodes.name: mixed
nodes.summary: Blends a stored pixel toward the tint color by the current amount, working channel by channel in the same steps the hardware blend uses.

nodes.name: laid
nodes.summary: Lays a see-through pixel over what is already there, so a transparent layer shows the layer behind it.

nodes.name: blend
nodes.summary: The shared channel-wise mix of two 15-bit colors by a step count, which both the fade and the see-through paths go through so the two agree step for step.

nodes.name: list_value.rb
nodes.summary: The interpreter's model of a `list`: a bounded, ordered collection backed by a plain Ruby array, matching the console on capacity, on when a push overflows, and on what a value too big for a narrow slot reads back as.
nodes.languageNotes: Only the observable behavior has to match the console's ring buffer, not the storage layout — but the width truncation does, so both backends drop the same bits.

nodes.name: ListValue
nodes.summary: Push, pop, shift, index and length over a capped array, with each stored value narrowed to the list's declared slot width.

nodes.name: fit
nodes.summary: Narrows a value to the list's slot width by keeping the low bits and sign-extending, exactly as the console does when a number is too big for a byte or half.

nodes.name: build.rb
nodes.summary: Readable constructors for every IR node kind — the layer the DSL and the tests build trees through, so callers name a kind and its operands tersely instead of learning the node's attribute conventions.
nodes.languageNotes: Trailing underscores on if_, loop_ and case_ because those words are Ruby keywords; the helpers also wrap bare literals into value nodes so callers can pass plain integers.

nodes.name: Build
nodes.summary: The module of node constructors, usable either as mixed-in methods or as Build.set(...) calls, covering drawing, sound, control flow, sprites, layers, lists, tables and expressions.

nodes.name: if_
nodes.summary: Builds a conditional node, splitting the trailing else branch out of the children and validating the frequency estimate a caller can attach.

nodes.name: list_new
nodes.summary: Builds a list declaration, validating the capacity, the slot width and the fast/roomy hint, and rounding the capacity up to a power of two when the list is ever shifted.

nodes.name: mul_fix
nodes.summary: Builds the wide fixed-point multiply used when two fractional numbers meet, which would otherwise overflow a 32-bit register on the way.

nodes.name: div_fix
nodes.summary: Builds the wide fixed-point divide — the perspective divide a first-person view is made of — which widens the numerator first so the answer keeps its fraction.

nodes.name: shift_right
nodes.summary: Builds a sign-preserving right shift, validating the bit count is in range.

nodes.name: wrap
nodes.summary: Turns whatever a caller passed — a plain integer, a symbol naming a variable, or an existing node — into a value node, which is what lets every constructor accept bare literals.

nodes.name: element_range
nodes.summary: The range a slot of a given width can hold — always signed, so a countdown that dips below zero reads back correctly rather than as a huge positive number.

nodes.name: round_up_capacity
nodes.summary: Rounds a shifted list's capacity up to the next power of two so the ring buffer's wrap is a single masking step.

nodes.name: buttons.rb
nodes.summary: The button vocabulary every backend agrees on — the ten Game Boy Advance button names a program may read with `held` or `pressed` — kept in the IR core so a typo becomes a plain error rather than a button that reads as never pressed.
nodes.languageNotes: Mirrors how color works: the IR carries the name and each backend maps it to its own world — a key bit on the console, set membership in the interpreter.

nodes.name: Buttons
nodes.summary: Holds the frozen list of button names and the membership check callers use before accepting one.

nodes.name: dump.rb
nodes.summary: Turns an IR tree back into runnable Ruby source that reconstructs it, so `ruby-gba build --format=ir` can hand back a self-contained file for inspecting or bisecting the compiler without a ROM in the way.
nodes.languageNotes: Generic over every node kind on purpose — it reads whatever operands a node carries and emits Nodes.build calls, which map one-for-one onto the stored shape, so a new IR feature needs nothing added here.

nodes.name: Dump
nodes.summary: Module functions that render a node, its operands, its children and the program's font registrations as Ruby source.

nodes.name: source
nodes.summary: Renders one node as a Nodes.build call with its operands and nested children, recursing through the whole subtree.

nodes.name: value_source
nodes.summary: Renders one operand value — a nested node, an array, a binary string or a plain literal — as Ruby source that reconstructs it exactly.

nodes.name: emit_class
nodes.summary: Wraps a dumped tree in a complete, runnable Ruby file — requires, font registrations, build flags and the program itself — so the dump can be executed straight back.

nodes.name: fields.rb
nodes.summary: A view over what each node kind carries, read off the classes that declare it, for the two callers that hold a kind's name rather than one of its nodes — the conformance coverage check and the cost model.
nodes.languageNotes: Deliberately a view rather than a table kept beside the declarations, so it cannot drift from them.

nodes.name: Fields
nodes.summary: Three module functions: every kind's operands by name, whether a kind is known, and the operands of one kind.

nodes.name: frames.rb
nodes.summary: The cross-backend contract for how many real frames one pass of the game loop answered for — the variable names and the cap on a single pass — so anything that must keep real time counts frames rather than passes.
nodes.languageNotes: A pass is one frame on a game that keeps up and two or three on one that does not; the cap stops a very late pass asking the game for half a second of catching up at once.

nodes.name: Frames
nodes.summary: The names of the frame counter, the mark at the top of the last pass, the step between them, and the most a single pass may answer for.

nodes.name: glyph_usage.rb
nodes.summary: The tree-shaking pass behind data-driven fonts: walks the program to find which glyphs each font can actually be asked to draw, so a big font used narrowly ships only the handful it really touches.
nodes.languageNotes: draw_text contributes its exact characters because the string is fixed at build time; draw_digit contributes the ten digits because a run-time number shows one of them.

nodes.name: GlyphUsage
nodes.summary: Returns the reachable glyph keys per font, plus a per-font footprint value object so the tree-shaking is visible in the build report.

nodes.name: reachable
nodes.summary: Walks every text and digit draw in the program, folding each one's characters through its font, and returns the sorted glyph keys each font may draw.

nodes.name: guardrails.rb
nodes.summary: The guardrail mechanism: a registry of checks, the Finding/Fix/Report value objects a check reports through, and the Validator pass that runs them over the IR before it is lowered. Also requires and lists the 27 built-in checks that carry the target knowledge.
nodes.languageNotes: Checking the semantic tree rather than finished machine code is what lets a message say "you drew but never turned the display on" instead of a black screen.

nodes.name: Guardrails
nodes.summary: The namespace and registry: registers, unregisters and lists checks, and assembles the default check list the build validates with.

nodes.name: Finding
nodes.summary: One problem a check found: its severity, its plain-language message, the node it blames so the author knows where to look, and an optional auto-applicable fix.
nodes.languageNotes: Data.define rather than Struct — a finding is never mutated after a check reports it.

nodes.name: Report
nodes.summary: The result of a validation pass: splits findings into errors and warnings, prints them with a heading and a count, and raises ValidationError when a real problem was not fixed.

nodes.name: Validator
nodes.summary: The pass itself: runs each check against the program, applies the safe fixes a finding offers, and gathers everything into one Report.

nodes.name: emit
nodes.summary: Prints the report — a heading saying how many problems and of what kind, then each finding's full message — the one path every guardrail message the developer reads goes through.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: Runs every registered check over the program, stepping a progress indicator, applying each finding's fix where one is offered, and returning the collected Report.

nodes.name: bitmap_draw_on_tiled.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a bitmap drawing call in an otherwise working tiled game: the tiled screen never reads the framebuffer, so the call runs every frame, costs its time and changes nothing on screen with no crash to say so.
nodes.languageNotes: Deliberately split from EmptyTiledScreen because the advice differs — this game HAS a background, so telling the author to switch to screen :bitmap would throw it away.

nodes.name: BitmapDrawOnTiled
nodes.summary: The check: finds bitmap draw ops sitting under a tiled display mode in a program the tile hardware is actually painting for, and names the verb that will do nothing.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Resolves the program's display modes, bails out when nothing tiled is being painted, then reports every bitmap draw whose enclosing mode is a tile-hardware one.

nodes.name: message
nodes.summary: Writes the plain-language explanation, naming the verb the author wrote and pointing at the tiled way to do the same thing.

nodes.name: call_inside_area.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail refusing a call to a drawing routine from inside an `inside` block: the console bakes the clip into the routine's own instructions wherever it was lowered, never at the call site, so the two backends would show a different picture with nothing crashing to say so.
nodes.languageNotes: The fix is always available — move the `inside` block inside the routine, so the clip travels with the routine everywhere it is called from.

nodes.name: CallInsideArea
nodes.summary: The check: indexes the program's routines, then reports any call inside a clip area whose target draws something the area was supposed to clip.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Collects the program's routines by name, then reports every call found inside an `inside` block whose routine draws.

nodes.name: unclipped_draw_in
nodes.summary: Walks a routine's body, following further calls, to find the first draw op that an area would have clipped — guarding against cycles as it goes.

nodes.name: channel_conflict.rb
nodes.summary: Advisory guardrail for a two-part song played in a game that also beeps: the song's second part and `beep` share the only remaining sound voice, so the two keep cutting each other off, silently and baffingly if you do not know the console has so few voices.
nodes.languageNotes: A warning rather than an error — the ROM still builds, and the two really can share the voice if the interruption is acceptable.

nodes.name: ChannelConflict
nodes.summary: The check: looks for a beep alongside a played song that has two voices, and names the songs involved.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Returns nothing unless the program beeps, then finds which of the songs it actually plays are layered two-part ones.

nodes.name: dropped_frame_sync.rb
nodes.summary: Advisory guardrail saying where a `wait_vblank` written inside a game loop went: under automatic frame sync the loop already opens each pass with the frame boundary, so the wait is counted rather than emitted — two waits a pass would run the game at half speed.
nodes.languageNotes: Reports from a count rather than from the tree, because a counted wait leaves no node behind to find — it still runs as an ordinary check so every message reaches the developer on the one report path.

nodes.name: DroppedFrameSync
nodes.summary: The check: constructed with how many waits the game loop already covered, and reports a warning when that count is above zero.

nodes.name: empty_tiled_screen.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a tiled screen with no background and no sprite — the classic silent black screen, usually hit by switching one line of a working bitmap game to `screen :tiled` while every draw call keeps painting a framebuffer nothing shows any more.
nodes.languageNotes: Splits its advice two ways: tell an author who is still drawing the bitmap way to change the screen line back, and tell one who drew nothing at all that there is nothing for the tile hardware to paint.

nodes.name: EmptyTiledScreen
nodes.summary: The check: decides whether the program is a mode conversion that kept its bitmap draws or a tiled game that declared nothing to paint, and writes the matching message.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Returns nothing when the screen has anything to paint, otherwise picks between the wrong-screen message and the nothing-to-show message.

nodes.name: wrong_screen
nodes.summary: The message for a bitmap game converted by one line: names a draw verb the program still uses and says to change the screen line back.

nodes.name: nothing_to_show
nodes.summary: The message for a tiled screen that declared no background and no sprite, explaining that the tile hardware has nothing to paint and what to add.

nodes.name: fade_never_lifted.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a screen faded all the way out and never brought back — the picture is all still there underneath, which is what makes it hard to spot, and the usual way in is fading out for a scene change and forgetting the fade in.
nodes.languageNotes: Only judges a fade whose amount is a number written in the program; a fade driven by a variable is how a fade over time is written and where it ends up cannot be known here.

nodes.name: FadeNeverLifted
nodes.summary: The check: looks at the program's fades, and reports when the last one written with a fixed amount leaves the screen completely covered, describing what that fade covers.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Gathers the fades whose amount is a plain number and reports the last one when it reaches the level where nothing shows through.

nodes.name: what_it_covers
nodes.summary: Describes in plain words how much of the screen the fade hides, accounting for a fade placed at a layer in the stack rather than over everything.

nodes.name: frame_from_cartridge.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the footgun where the game loop's body grows too large to fit in the console's 32K of fast on-chip memory, so the whole frame runs from the slow cartridge at roughly 2.5x the cost. It warns with the exact byte shortfall and tells the author to move the bulky, rarely-run code into its own `func` marked `fast: false`.
nodes.languageNotes: Reads the code-placement chooser's `passed_over` record rather than re-deriving it, so the warning and the actual placement decision can never disagree.

nodes.name: FrameFromCartridge
nodes.summary: Check class that reports when the per-frame routine was passed over for fast memory. Constructed with the build's Placement record; emits one warning naming the bytes needed versus the bytes free at the moment the loop's turn came.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Looks up the frame routine in the placement's passed-over list and pairs it with the program's `loop` node, returning a single warning Finding. Stays silent when no chooser ran (a `fast_code: false` build passes nothing over).

nodes.name: frame_reach.rb
nodes.summary: Shared frame-path analysis used by several per-frame guardrails: it answers "what does this game loop actually run every frame?" once, instead of each check re-implementing the walk. It follows call and case dispatch into funcs but deliberately stops at a `pressed`-guarded body, since a press fires once in a while rather than steadily.

nodes.name: FrameReach
nodes.summary: A `module_function` module exposing the steady-per-frame traversal: `loops` finds every endless loop, `index_funcs` maps func names to nodes, and `steady_statements` collects everything reachable each frame. Centralizing it keeps RedrawEverything and SpriteClearedEachFrame from drifting apart on what "every frame" means.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses Ruby's `module_function` so the methods are callable as `FrameReach.steady_statements(...)` without instantiation.

nodes.name: steady_statements
nodes.summary: Recursively accumulates every statement reachable on a normal frame from a node, descending through `call` targets and `case` clause targets into func bodies. Returns immediately on a transition node (an `if` whose condition is `pressed`), which is what keeps once-per-round setup out of the steady path.

nodes.name: iwram_budget.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the footgun of declaring more state than the console physically has, checking two real ceilings: that what can only live in fast memory (variables and sprite save-under buffers) fits in the usable 28K, and that everything declared fits in fast plus roomy memory combined. It errors with the total needed, the memory available, and the three biggest users, so the fix (smaller capacity, fewer fields, `width: :byte`) is obvious.
nodes.languageNotes: Distinguishes movable state (lists and pools, which can fall into the 256K external RAM) from pinned state (variables, reached by a fixed offset from the fast memory's base, which is what makes a variable read two instructions instead of four).

nodes.name: IwramBudget
nodes.summary: Check class that totals every byte a program reserves and compares it against the two hardware memories. Holds the constants for the ceilings (32K fast RAM minus a 4K reserve for the call stack, 256K roomy RAM) and builds the two error messages, one for the pinned overflow and one for the combined overflow.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Sums the contributors, splits them into pinned and movable, and raises the pinned-overflow error first (no other memory can take that state) before checking the combined total. Blames the biggest user's declaration node so the author lands on the line worth shrinking.

nodes.name: contributors
nodes.summary: Builds the list of everything reserving memory as label/bytes/node/movable records, largest first: lists and pools, one word per distinct variable name, and the sprite save-under buffers. Variables and buffers carry no single declaration node, so they are marked unmovable and nodeless and blame the program itself.

nodes.name: list_declarations
nodes.summary: Walks every `list_new` node and sizes it at its own element width, so a byte-wide list is counted as the quarter of the memory it really takes. Adds two hidden bookkeeping words per list and dedupes by name, so a list re-declared to reset it is only charged once.

nodes.name: layer_holds_nothing.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a layer named in the `layers` stack that nothing was ever put into. Nothing breaks, which is the point: the stack is the one line a reader trusts for what sits in front of what, so a name that means nothing reads as an answer and is not one. It warns and says to either fill the layer with a `layer` block or drop the name.
nodes.languageNotes: Also consults the build's software sprite handles, because a software sprite's layer lives on the handle rather than in the IR tree — a tree-only walk would call such a layer empty.

nodes.name: LayerHoldsNothing
nodes.summary: Whole-program check that subtracts the layers actually in use from the declared stack. Phrases two different messages: one for a few stray names (likely a spelling slip or an edit that moved the last thing out) and one for the case where every declared layer is empty.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Finds the `layers` declaration, subtracts the in-use layer names from the declared ones, and emits a single warning blaming the stack declaration itself. A layer named only as the line an effect sits under (`fade ... under: :cut`) counts as in use.

nodes.name: layer_invisible.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a layer declared `transparency: 100`, which means none of it shows — the same picture as not declaring the layer at all, except the game still holds its art, its tiles and a level of hardware depth. Almost always a slider walked the wrong way (0 is solid, 100 invisible), so it warns and restates which end is which.

nodes.name: LayerInvisible
nodes.summary: Check class that fires only on a transparency the author wrote as a plain 100. It says nothing about an amount the game works out, because a variable passing through 100 for one frame of thickening fog is the effect working correctly.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Scans for a `layers` node whose transparency resolves to the fixed number 100 and emits one warning naming the layer. Uses `Value.fixed_number` so a runtime-computed amount returns nil and is skipped.

nodes.name: layer_solid_while_fading.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a game that both fades the screen and sees through a layer. Both use the display's single blend unit, so the see-through layer goes solid while a fade runs and comes back when it lifts — invisible from the code, since the two verbs are written in different places. It warns rather than refuses, and points at `tint`/`flash_screen`, which mix by a different route and leave the layer blending.

nodes.name: LayerSolidWhileFading
nodes.summary: Check class pairing a blending `layers` node with any `fade` node. Its `blends?` helper treats a layer fixed at 0 as already solid (nothing for a fade to take) but asks about a runtime amount, since one worth writing will not stay at 0.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Returns a single warning when the program contains both a blending layer and a fade, blaming the fade node (the verb whose reach is surprising). Silent when either half is missing.

nodes.name: list_in_loop.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the one-time-setup footgun of declaring `list :name, capacity:` inside a per-frame context, where the declaration re-runs and re-creates the list empty every frame, so anything pushed is thrown away and the length never grows. No crash, just a collection that mysteriously refuses to fill; it warns and says to declare the list in setup and only push/read inside the loop.

nodes.name: ListInLoop
nodes.summary: Check class mixing in PerFrameScope to reuse the shared per-frame-container detection, so it only has to say which verb it cares about (`list_new`) and how to phrase the fix. Flags only unconditional declarations, leaving a list created inside a condition (a deliberate reset) alone.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Walks for `list_new` nodes whose direct parent is a per-frame container (the game loop, a repeat, an every timer, or a per-frame func) and emits one warning each. Checking the direct parent is what restricts it to unconditional declarations.

nodes.name: manual_sprite_blit.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the double-drawn-sprite footgun: hand-blitting an image that is already a sprite. The sprite redraws itself and restores the pixels beneath, while the hand `blit` stamps a second copy nothing ever erases, so it smears exactly the trail the sprite was chosen to avoid. It warns and says to move the sprite's x/y instead, or give the plain stamp a different image name.

nodes.name: ManualSpriteBlit
nodes.summary: Check class that recognizes a sprite structurally with no build-time bookkeeping: a blit sitting beside a save/restore-region op is the framework's own draw, since nothing else emits those ops. Any other blit of the same image is one the author wrote by hand.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Classifies the program's blits, then emits a warning for every blit of a sprite-managed image that is not itself one of the framework's draws. Identity (`object_id`) separates the sprite's own repaint from a hand-written blit of the same image.

nodes.name: classify_blits
nodes.summary: Walks every container and, where a save/restore-region op sits among the children, records both the image names those siblings manage and the object identities of the framework's own blits. Returns the two sets so the caller can tell a sprite's draw from a hand one.

nodes.name: off_screen_draw.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a draw whose whole footprint lands off the 240x160 screen and therefore paints nothing — the "why is my sprite missing" mystery with no crash to point at. A partly off-screen draw is intentional and stays silent; only a fully off-screen one warns, naming the position, size and the screen's real corners, and suggesting a swapped x and y.
nodes.languageNotes: Only build-time-constant positions are checkable; a draw placed at a variable position is decided (and safely clipped) at run time, so it is skipped here.

nodes.name: OffScreenDraw
nodes.summary: Check class that computes a constant bounding box for each kind of draw op — pixel, rect, text (via the font's measured width), digit, and blit (sized from the indexed bitmap) — and tests it against the screen box. Also phrases the message subject per kind so each finding opens with a proper noun.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Indexes the embedded bitmaps for sizing, then emits a warning for every node whose fully-known footprint misses the screen entirely. Nodes with a runtime position yield no bounds and are skipped.

nodes.name: constant_bounds
nodes.summary: Dispatches on node kind to produce [x, y, w, h] for a draw whose whole footprint is known at build time, or nil when the node is not a positioned draw or its coordinates are runtime values. Text and digit footprints come from the font's metrics; a blit's comes from its image, not the blit op.

nodes.name: describe
nodes.summary: Returns the plain-language subject for a finding's first sentence, per draw kind — "A pixel", "A filled rectangle", the quoted text or image name. Keeps every message opening with a capital like the rest of the guardrail findings.

nodes.name: orphaned_condition.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the native-`if` slip: a DSL comparison is a Condition object, and Ruby treats any object as truthy, so `if x > 5` runs its body every time with the comparison silently ignored. It errors (there is no legitimate cause to weigh against) and says to branch with `(x > 5).then { ... }` instead.
nodes.languageNotes: Cannot detect by walking the IR — an unused Condition records no node — so the builder tracks a pending set and hands the leftovers here, letting it still run as an ordinary check with no special path.

nodes.name: OrphanedCondition
nodes.summary: Check class constructed with the Conditions the builder built but never branched on. Turns each leftover into an error Finding that blames the Condition itself, since it carries the author's call site and there is no tree node to point at.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Maps the pending Condition set to Findings, ignoring the program entirely — its data is the leftover set rather than the tree. The ignored argument is what lets it sit in the Validator's ordinary check list.

nodes.name: finding
nodes.summary: Class method building the error Finding for one unused Condition, carrying the plain-language explanation of why a native Ruby `if` on a Condition always runs its body and how `.then` fixes it. Standalone so tests can assert the message directly.

nodes.name: orphaned_expression.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the `|=` slip and everything shaped like it: `flags | MASK` builds a new number nobody keeps, and `flags |= MASK` rebinds the Ruby local while the game's variable stays untouched — with the name still looking right afterwards. The same hole swallows `hp + 1` where `hp.add 1` was meant. It errors and shows the `flags.set flags | 4` form.
nodes.languageNotes: Needs no consume-bookkeeping: writing a node into another node wires its parent back, so an expression that found a home has a parent and an orphan has none. That test only works because the framework builds no throwaway expressions of its own.

nodes.name: OrphanedExpression
nodes.summary: Check class constructed with every expression Value the build made; the unparented ones are the orphans. Reports errors rather than warnings, since an expression built and dropped did nothing at all and, unlike a statement, has no effect to be had.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Rejects every expression whose node has a parent and turns the rest into error Findings. The program is not consulted, because an orphan is precisely what is missing from it.

nodes.name: finding
nodes.summary: Class method building the error Finding for one thrown-away expression, spelling out that `flags | 4` returns a new number, that `flags |= 4` moves only the Ruby name, and that `.set` / `.add` are what change the game's variable. Standalone so the message is easy to assert.

nodes.name: per_frame_scope.rb
nodes.summary: Shared machinery for the one-time-setup guardrails, which are all the same shape: a verb meant to run once, written directly inside a per-frame context where it silently re-runs every frame. It identifies those contexts so each check only has to name its verb and phrase its fix.

nodes.name: PerFrameScope
nodes.summary: Mixin defining what counts as a per-frame container (the game loop, a repeat, an every timer, a per-frame func) and providing plain-language names for the message. Deliberately excludes `after` (one-shot) and `.then` conditionals, so only a direct unconditional statement of a per-frame body is ever flagged.

nodes.name: per_frame_func_names
nodes.summary: Computes the transitive closure of funcs reached by unconditional calls from inside per-frame loops, using a worklist over the func index. A call guarded by a condition or an input edge is excluded, which is what keeps a one-off reset routine from being mistaken for per-frame setup.

nodes.name: per_frame_where
nodes.summary: Returns a plain-language phrase for where an offending op sits — "your game loop", "a repeat loop", "an every(...) timer", or the scene/routine by name. Strips the internal `_scene_` prefix so the message shows the name the author typed.

nodes.name: redraw_everything.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the tearing footgun in its high-signal form: a game loop that clears the whole screen every frame and also repaints a collection that grows as the game runs (a snake's body, a list of shots), so the redraw gets heavier until it no longer fits the console's brief window to change the screen. It warns and prescribes incremental drawing — paint the board once per round, then each frame touch only the cells that change.
nodes.languageNotes: Stays silent on a double-buffered program: drawing goes to a hidden page shown all at once, so a full repaint cannot tear (its worst case is a frame-rate drop, which the draw-budget check owns).

nodes.name: RedrawEverything
nodes.summary: Check class matching the structural pattern (a clear plus an unbounded list-length repeat that paints) on the steady per-frame path only. It is the cheap companion to the cost estimator — no weights, just the pattern — so it carries near-zero false positives.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Bails out early on a buffered screen, then for each game loop collects the steady statements and warns when they contain both a `clear_screen` and a repeat over a list's length whose body paints. Work behind a `pressed` edge is excluded by the steady walk, so a board painted once on START is correctly left alone.

nodes.name: screen_mode_set.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the classic silent-black-screen footgun: the program draws but never picks a screen mode, and on the Game Boy Advance nothing appears until a mode is chosen, so the whole game runs invisibly with no crash to diagnose. Since the fix is completely safe, it also ships an auto-fix that prepends `screen :bitmap` and leaves a warning explaining what was added.
nodes.languageNotes: Also holds the doc comment for the whole Checks namespace: unlike the registry in guardrails.rb, a check encodes real hardware knowledge, so this is where target-specific footgun detail is allowed to live.

nodes.name: ScreenModeSet
nodes.summary: Check class holding both messages — the problem statement and the text shown after the auto-fix applies — plus the fix itself, which rebuilds the program with a bitmap `screen` ahead of every existing statement. Nags only a program that actually draws and has no `screen` op anywhere.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Finds the program's first drawing op (excluding `screen` itself, which is categorized as a draw), returns nothing if a mode is already set, and otherwise emits an error Finding carrying a Fix. Blames the first draw, since that is the line the missing `screen` has to go above.

nodes.name: seed_in_loop.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the RNG one-time-setup footgun: `seed` written directly inside a per-frame context re-runs every frame and keeps resetting the stream to the same point, so every "random" draw returns the same value and enemies, item drops and rolls freeze. It warns and says to move the seed to setup, or call `randomize` instead while waiting for input.
nodes.languageNotes: It teaches rather than silently hoisting, because a game may deliberately re-seed from something the player influences — unlike `var`, whose initial value is now applied once wherever it is written.

nodes.name: SeedInLoop
nodes.summary: Check class mixing in PerFrameScope. Tells a re-seed from a churn structurally: a churn (roll/rand/randomize) advances the stream by reading it, so it references the state variable, while a re-seed replaces the state outright and does not. It reads the state variable's name from the Randomness builder so the two cannot drift.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Walks for `set` nodes that assign the RNG state without reading it and whose direct parent is a per-frame container, emitting one warning each. A seed gated by a condition or an input edge is a deliberate re-seed and is left alone.

nodes.name: sprite_cleared_each_frame.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the sprite-that-gets-wiped footgun: a game loop that repaints a sprite and also clears the whole screen every frame. The two contradict each other — the sprite restores the pixels beneath itself, and the clear erases the field it just put back along with the sprite, so it flickers or vanishes and the tearing the sprite avoided returns. It warns and says to paint the field once, before the loop.

nodes.name: SpriteClearedEachFrame
nodes.summary: Check class recognizing a sprite structurally by the save/restore-region ops only a sprite's repaint emits, then looking for a whole-screen wipe on the same steady path — a `clear_screen`, or a fill covering the full 240x160 display. A pure pattern match, so near-zero false positives.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: For each game loop, checks the steady statements for sprite ops and then for a full-screen clear, blaming the clear rather than the loop — deleting that one line is the fix. Because the steady walk follows calls, the offending clear may sit in a scene some way from the loop.

nodes.name: stack_not_honored.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a layer stack a bitmap screen cannot show. A `background` on a bitmap screen stamps its tiles straight into the single picture where it is declared, so no later ordering can move it; sprites are exempt, since they are repainted every frame in stack order. It warns only when the two orders actually differ, and then prints both — what the stack asks for and what the screen will show.
nodes.languageNotes: Rescues Modes::Conflict and stays silent: when one drawing routine is reached from two screen modes, that error names it and there is no single mode in which to judge the picture.

nodes.name: StackNotHonored
nodes.summary: Check class comparing the true paint order against the order the stack asks for, using Stacking.order. Constructed with the build's software sprites in declaration order, because a sprite's layer lives on its handle rather than in the IR tree.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Finds the `layers` declaration, computes the painted order and the asked-for order, and warns only when they differ by identity at some index. Fewer than two stacked things come back unmoved, so the comparison answers "nothing to say" without a special case.

nodes.name: painted_in_order
nodes.summary: Builds the true paint order for a bitmap screen: bitmap-mode backgrounds in declaration order (they stamp where declared and nothing later can move them), then the sprites already sorted into stack order by the frame boundary. Resolves each background's mode through Modes so a mixed-mode program is judged correctly.

nodes.name: termination.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a program whose top-level flow just ends — no `halt`, no forever-running `game_loop` — after which the console executes whatever bytes come next in memory, which is garbage. The classic case is a static picture program that forgets to `halt`; it warns at the last statement that runs and names both fixes.
nodes.languageNotes: Reading termination off the IR is exact where scanning finished machine code was a heuristic: top-level statements run unconditionally in order, so the program stops if and only if one of them never returns.

nodes.name: Termination
nodes.summary: Check class that skips definition nodes (func, define_sound, song, data, bitmap emit nothing in line) when judging the flow, then asks whether any executed statement never returns. Treats a `raw` block as opaque and possibly terminating, preferring silence to a wrong warning.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Returns nothing when the program has no executable flow (the no-code check's job) or when some statement never returns; otherwise warns at the last statement that runs, which is the line control falls off the end of and where the missing `halt` goes.

nodes.name: never_returns?
nodes.summary: Decides whether reaching a statement means control never falls through: a halt, an always-infinite loop or a raw block stop for good, and a call stops only if its target func never returns. A seen set guards against a call cycle.

nodes.name: tiled_display.rb
nodes.summary: Shared vocabulary for what the tiled display can and cannot put on screen, so the two checks that ask it the same questions — "is anything painting here?" and "is this a draw only the bitmap screen understands?" — can never drift apart on the answer. The tiled screen keeps no framebuffer: it paints tile images arranged by a map plus composited sprites, and nothing else reaches the display.

nodes.name: TiledDisplay
nodes.summary: A `module_function` module holding two lists — PAINTS (background and object, the only things tile hardware shows) and BITMAP_DRAWS (framebuffer-only ops a tiled screen never displays) — plus `paints?` and a verb-naming helper delegating to PlainWords. Keying on those kinds is safe because the DSL has already chosen by the time the tree exists: text and sprites on a tiled screen record `object` nodes, never these.

nodes.name: tint_never_lifted.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a screen tinted all the way and never brought back. A full tint mixes its color in completely, so nothing shows through — not the game, not a sprite, not anything drawn afterwards — while the picture is all still there underneath, which is what makes it hard to spot. It warns and says to use an amount of 0 when the tint is finished.
nodes.languageNotes: A separate check from the fade's twin rather than a branch inside it, so the advice names the verb the author actually wrote. A tint driven by a variable is skipped entirely — where it ends up is not knowable at build time.

nodes.name: TintNeverLifted
nodes.summary: Check class holding the FULL threshold (100, the amount at which nothing shows through) and the single warning message. Reads each tint's amount only when it is a plain integer literal, returning nil for a runtime value.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Collects every tint's amount and bails out on three conditions before warning: any runtime amount (unknowable), any amount of zero (something does bring it back), or a maximum below 100. Blames the last tint node.

nodes.name: vblank_sync.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a game loop that never waits for the screen's vertical blank, so it runs thousands of passes a second instead of 60: the picture tears, the loop spins for nothing, and frame-based logic like edge-detected input and the music sequencer races. The classic report is "my game runs way too fast"; it advises adding `wait_vblank` as the loop's first line.
nodes.languageNotes: Soft and advisory rather than an error, because there are legitimate reasons to have no wait_vblank — a raw block hand-rolling its own sync, or a deliberate benchmark loop.

nodes.name: VblankSync
nodes.summary: Check class testing reachability rather than direct children, since a game may sync inside a scene it dispatches to rather than in the loop body itself. Holds the single PROBLEM message and the func index used to follow calls.

nodes.name: detect
nodes.summary: Indexes the funcs, then emits one warning per game loop from which no frame sync is reachable, blaming the loop node itself.

nodes.name: reaches_sync?
nodes.summary: Walks a node's whole subtree looking for a `wait_vblank`, following `call` and `case` dispatch into the funcs they target. A reachable `raw` block counts as synced — it is opaque and may hand-roll a sync, and staying quiet beats crying wolf; a seen set guards a call cycle.

nodes.name: int32.rb
nodes.summary: The IR's reference integer semantics — signed 32-bit two's-complement with wraparound — defined as a cross-backend contract rather than a hardware detail, so the ARM lowering and the Ruby interpreter can never subtly disagree. Every backend routes its arithmetic through here, including the fixed-point multiply and divide that must form their intermediate at full width to avoid overflow.
nodes.languageNotes: Pins several deliberate divergences from Ruby: `/` truncates toward zero (matching the console's BIOS Div) while `%` keeps Ruby's sign-of-divisor meaning for wrapping, and a negative or >=32 shift count empties the number instead of reversing direction as Ruby does.

nodes.name: Int32
nodes.summary: A `module_function` module defining every arithmetic, bitwise, shift and comparison operation the IR recognizes, all normalized through a single `wrap`. Holds the 32-bit constants (MASK, MIN, MAX, BITS) so "what wrapping means" is stated in exactly one place.

nodes.name: wrap
nodes.summary: Normalizes any Ruby integer to a signed 32-bit value: masks to the low 32 bits, then reads the top bit as the sign so 0x8000_0000 becomes MIN rather than a large positive. Every other operation in the module routes through it.

nodes.name: mul_fix
nodes.summary: Multiplies two numbers that each carry the same fraction bits and shifts the doubled-up scale back out. Forms the product at full width first, because the intermediate overflows 32 bits (1.5 x 1.5 at 16 fraction bits needs 9,663,676,416) where plain `mul` would wrap and return nonsense.

nodes.name: div_fix
nodes.summary: Divides two fixed-point numbers, widening the numerator by the fraction bits first so the answer keeps its scale — the mirror of mul_fix's problem. Clamps rather than wraps on overflow, because dividing by a near-zero distance should give the tallest wall the numbers allow, not a negative one that draws nothing.

nodes.name: shift_right
nodes.summary: Arithmetic right shift: divides by a power of two rounding down toward minus infinity, not toward zero, which is exactly what dropping the low bits of a fixed-point number does and keeps conversion and multiplication agreeing at the boundary. An out-of-range count empties the number to 0 or -1 depending on the sign.

nodes.name: div
nodes.summary: Signed division truncated toward zero, matching the console's BIOS Div and C rather than Ruby's flooring `/`. Divides the magnitudes and reapplies the sign, which is what avoids Ruby stepping to the whole number on the left for negatives.

nodes.name: mod
nodes.summary: Remainder with Ruby's meaning (sign of the divisor), deliberately not the one implied by `div`. That is what wrapping wants — an angle one step below zero is one below a full turn — since a remainder of -1 would index off the front of every table it was used on. Raises a plain-language ZeroDivisionError.

nodes.name: modes.rb
nodes.summary: Works out which screen mode each scene of a program runs in, so a bitmap title can hand off to a tear-free play field and the framework switches the hardware as each scene takes over. Pure structural analysis of the program with no target machine assumed, which lets the backend and the cost/palette analyses all read one answer instead of each deriving it and risking a subtle disagreement.
nodes.languageNotes: A drawing routine reached from two different modes cannot draw both ways, so it raises Modes::Conflict — a friendly error rather than a silently wrong screen.

nodes.name: Modes
nodes.summary: Resolves and then answers questions about the program's screen modes: the four mode constants (direct, buffered, tiled, affine), the boot mode, a func-name to mode map, the scene entry points, and predicates like `any_buffered?`, `any_tiled?`, `mixed?` and `mixed_display?`. `mode_at` reports the mode in force where any statement sits, which is what lets one program be judged scene by scene.

nodes.name: initialize
nodes.summary: Indexes the funcs, determines the boot mode, then resolves the case_var dispatch targets as scenes and every other main-body call target as a non-scene. That split matters: a bare per-frame helper such as once_a_frame's hidden routine gets a mode but no mode-switch preamble, which would otherwise re-enter its own mode every frame and clear a real scene's sprites before the console ever showed them.

nodes.name: resolve_func
nodes.summary: Assigns a func the mode it declares or the one it was reached in, records it as a scene when appropriate, and recurses into its own call targets. Raises Modes::Conflict with a plain-language message when the same func is reached at two different modes.

nodes.name: declared_mode
nodes.summary: Reads the screen mode a run of statements declares via a `screen` node among them: tiled for a tiled screen, affine for rotozoom, else buffered or direct depending on the double-buffering flag. Returns nil when no mode is declared, so the caller falls back to the inherited one.

nodes.name: mode_at
nodes.summary: Walks up a statement's parent chain to the enclosing func and returns that func's resolved mode, or the boot mode for a statement in the main body. Asking per statement is what lets a bitmap title screen and a tiled play scene coexist and be judged apart.

nodes.name: buffered_scopes
nodes.summary: Returns the statement subtrees that draw in buffered mode — the main body when the boot mode is buffered, plus every reachable func resolved to buffered. The palette analysis walks exactly these, so a direct-color scene's colors never count toward the buffered screen's shared color table.

nodes.name: node.rb
nodes.summary: Defines the behavior every node of the intermediate representation shares: children, parent back-references, walking, categories, structural equality, deep copy and hashing. A node is plain Ruby data — no machine code, no output buffer — which is what lets the tree be built, walked and checked for footguns entirely in memory before any lowering pass exists.
nodes.languageNotes: A mixin that names no kind: each kind is its own class declaring what it is and what it carries, so adding a kind is adding a class and nothing else. Control flow is structured nesting rather than jumps, so labels and branch targets live only in the backend that flattens the tree.

nodes.name: Node
nodes.summary: The shared node mixin. Distinguishes statement nodes (the program itself, holding nested statements in children) from value nodes (expression operands living in another node's operand slots), and offers shape predicates — `sized?`, `colored?`, `branching?` — so a walk can ask what a node is in the words of the thing being asked about rather than probing for field names.

nodes.name: Declarations
nodes.summary: The class-level DSL each node kind uses to declare itself in three lines: its `kind` symbol, its `category`, and its `operands` with what each must hold. One declaration produces both the accessors and the tags the Verifier checks, so a field cannot be readable but unchecked, or checked but unreadable.

nodes.name: operands
nodes.summary: Stores the operand tags and defines a reader and a writer for each name. The generated writer wires a node-valued operand's parent back to the owner, so the tree stays navigable in both directions however it was assembled — a branch attached after its owner, a sprite given an angle once something turns it.

nodes.name: add_child
nodes.summary: Attaches a nested statement, rejecting a non-node with a clear ArgumentError and wiring the child's parent back-reference. Aliased as `<<` and returns the child so calls can chain.

nodes.name: walk
nodes.summary: Depth-first traversal over the entire tree — statement children plus any value nodes nested in the operands, directly or inside arrays. This is what a validation pass wants, as opposed to `each`, which visits statements only.

nodes.name: copy
nodes.summary: Produces a separate tree of the same shape with all-new objects and parents rewired to the copy, so the two trees share nothing. Exists for anything that has to change a program to learn about it — measuring a frame rate means adding a counter — leaving the original program intact.

nodes.name: to_h
nodes.summary: Renders the node and its subtree as a plain nested Hash for test assertions and the inspector's pretty-printing. Parent and source are intentionally omitted so the hash captures shape rather than identity, which is also what makes it the basis of `==` and `hash`.

nodes.name: set_operand
nodes.summary: Assigns an operand by name during construction, refusing an unknown name with an InvariantError that lists the fields the kind does have. The bare NoMethodError a writer would raise says nothing about the alternatives, and the answer is nearly always in that list.

nodes.name: nodes.rb
nodes.summary: One class per kind of IR node — roughly ninety of them covering every DSL verb's tree form: drawing (pixel, blit, draw_column_at, fade, tint), variables and arithmetic (set, binop, mul_fix, shift_right), control flow (loop, repeat, case, func, inside), lists, sound, and data. Each declares its kind, its category and its operands in three lines, so asking a pixel for its width is a NoMethodError at the line that asked rather than a nil that travels.
nodes.languageNotes: Several operand slots (`usually`, `most`, `over`/`of`, `runs`/`per`) are author estimates rather than program semantics — nothing runs differently either way. The `by_kind` registry is derived from the constants rather than kept alongside them, so it cannot fall behind.

nodes.name: Nodes
nodes.summary: The namespace holding every node kind class plus the two registry methods that turn a kind symbol into a class and build an instance from it. Each contained class mixes in Node and names its kind, category and operands; the shared behavior is known to none of them.

nodes.name: by_kind
nodes.summary: Memoizes a kind-symbol to class map derived by reflecting over the module's own constants, so a class that exists is automatically in the registry and the table cannot fall behind the definitions above it.

nodes.name: build
nodes.summary: The one place a kind symbol becomes a class: looks the kind up in the registry, raising a named ArgumentError for an unknown one, and constructs the node with the given children, source and operands. For callers that hold a name rather than a type.

nodes.name: palette.rb
nodes.summary: Target-agnostic IR pass that walks a finished program, collects every distinct color it actually draws, and assigns each a slot in the 256-entry indexed-display palette. Keeps the framework's promise that a game author writes color names and never learns that the tear-free screen stores an index per pixel.
nodes.languageNotes: Three friendly build errors are modelled as nested exception classes (Overflow, Missing, Conflict) so the caller can tell a too-many-colors program from one drawing outside a supplied table.

nodes.name: Palette
nodes.summary: Builds and holds the color-to-slot mapping for an indexed screen: #entries is the table a backend uploads, #index_of(color) the number to write per pixel. Either derives the table from the colors the program draws (black reserved at slot 0) or adopts one the program supplied verbatim.

nodes.name: indices_for
nodes.summary: Converts a picture's packed 15-bit pixels into one palette byte per pixel, plus the number that means 'leave this pixel alone'. The conversion nothing can be drawn on the indexed screen without.

nodes.name: collect
nodes.summary: Walks the given IR subtrees WHOLE (not just statement children) gathering every distinct color in first-seen order, from both the draw verbs' color specs and bitmap nodes' packed pixels.

nodes.name: parity.rb
nodes.summary: Proves whether a value the game works out is always even, always odd, or could be either — so a backend can emit one shape of code instead of both and pick at run time. A fact about the program, not the machine, which is why it lives in the IR core.
nodes.languageNotes: The design rule is that nil ('either, as far as this can tell') is the default for every unproven kind and operator, because claiming 'even' about an odd number would make a backend emit wrong code.

nodes.name: Parity
nodes.summary: Module of pure predicates answering :even, :odd or nil for an Integer or a value Node, folding through negation, addition, subtraction, multiplication and modulo.

nodes.name: of
nodes.summary: The entry point: answers :even, :odd or nil for an Integer or an IR value node. Anything it cannot see through falls through to nil.

nodes.name: of_binop
nodes.summary: The rules for a binary operation: sums and differences need both sides known, a product is even if either side is (which is what proves `cell * 8` even without knowing `cell`), and modulo answers only when both sides are even.

nodes.name: portability.rb
nodes.summary: The single source of truth tagging every IR node kind :portable or :hardware_only, so a preflight can say up front that a program uses `raw` and only runs on the console. A program's tier is the floor over its nodes.
nodes.languageNotes: The north star written into the comments is that `raw` should be the only lasting hardware-only kind — every other reach for it signals a missing IR node.

nodes.name: Portability
nodes.summary: Holds the TIER table mapping each IR kind to its portability tier and the queries over it: #of, #portable?, #hardware_only?, #hardware_only_kinds and a program's overall tier. An unclassified kind raises rather than being assumed portable.

nodes.name: of
nodes.summary: The tier of a kind Symbol or a Node. Raises a pointed ArgumentError on an unclassified kind, so a new IR primitive with no tag is caught as drift rather than falsely promising it runs on the web.

nodes.name: printer.rb
nodes.summary: The one place that decides how a report line LOOKS — plain text for a file or a pipe, an ANSI green-to-red heatmap for a terminal — while the cost model hands each line only its meaning (how hot it is, whether it is a group heading).
nodes.languageNotes: Colour is opt-out via the no-color.org NO_COLOR convention and opt-in only for a real tty, so a report captured to a StringIO stays byte-for-byte plain.

nodes.name: Printer
nodes.summary: The shared base: the severity scale, the row layout constants both subclasses lay a line out with, and the factory that picks a plain or coloured printer for a given stream.

nodes.name: PlainPrinter
nodes.summary: Writes every line verbatim, ignoring severity and emphasis — byte-for-byte the output from before colours existed, so a captured or piped report is unchanged.

nodes.name: ColorPrinter
nodes.summary: Wraps each line in ANSI codes: a green-to-red tint by how much of the frame budget it uses, with group headings additionally bold and underlined under just the indent and label.

nodes.name: for
nodes.summary: Factory that returns a ColorPrinter or a PlainPrinter for a stream. `color: :auto` tints only for an interactive terminal with NO_COLOR unset; true and false force it either way.

nodes.name: heading
nodes.summary: Renders a group heading row: bold and tinted across the whole row, but underlined only under the lead indent and the label text, so no rule runs across the padding to the value column.

nodes.name: screen.rb
nodes.summary: The logical display every backend renders: 240x160 pixels, stated once in the IR core so the interpreter's framebuffer, the console's hardware constants and any future backend all size themselves from one source of truth.

nodes.name: Screen
nodes.summary: Two constants, WIDTH and HEIGHT, defining the screen a program draws to whichever backend runs it.

nodes.name: stacking.rb
nodes.summary: Turns a program's declared layer stack into a drawing order and a set of depth levels, in one place so a backend, a build check and a report can never disagree about which thing is in front. Things that named no layer keep the exact places they had.
nodes.languageNotes: Depth LEVELS are deliberately scarce and only scenery opens a new one, because a console's stacking hardware has few of them and sprites over a background can share one.

nodes.name: Stacking
nodes.summary: Module holding the stacking rule plus the Picture and Depths value objects read off a program: the declared stack, scenery and objects in draw order, each thing's depth level, and which things an effect placed under a layer leaves alone.

nodes.name: order
nodes.summary: Rearranges the layered items among the positions THEY occupied, leaving items that named no layer exactly where they were — the property that makes layers safe to adopt one part of a game at a time.

nodes.name: picture
nodes.summary: Reads everything about how a program's picture is stacked off the IR in one call — the declared stack, the scenery and objects in drawing order, and the depth of each — so every consumer gets the same answer.

nodes.name: depths
nodes.summary: Works out which depth level each named thing sits at, spending as few levels as the picture needs: only scenery opens a new one. A picture that names no layers falls out of the same rule unchanged.

nodes.name: merge
nodes.summary: Interleaves scenery and objects into one back-to-front sequence tagged by kind, with scenery first inside a shared layer and anything that named no layer taking its historic place (scenery at the back, objects in front).

nodes.name: at_or_above
nodes.summary: Everything at a named layer and in front of it — what an effect placed under that layer leaves alone. Read off the stack rather than the levels, since a background and the sprites over it share one level.

nodes.name: tile_map.rb
nodes.summary: Decides which fixed grid size (32 or 64 cells per axis) a tiled background scrolls over, which is not the same as how many rows the author wrote — so every backend agrees on where the picture comes round again.

nodes.name: TileMap
nodes.summary: Module answering the grid a background scrolls over, whether a map fits one at all, and the biggest map there is — derived from the authored map and nothing else.

nodes.name: grid
nodes.summary: The grid a background scrolls over as [columns, rows], each rounded up to the smallest supported size that holds the authored cells.

nodes.name: verifier.rb
nodes.summary: A well-formedness pass that mechanically enforces the IR value model — every operand is a value node, every structural slot an author-time literal — instead of trusting each DSL verb to remember it. A failure is a ruby-gba bug, never a game author's mistake.
nodes.languageNotes: Deliberately distinct from Guardrails::ValidationError: an InvariantError is never shown to a game developer and offers no fix, because the developer could not have caused it.

nodes.name: Verifier
nodes.summary: Walks a program tree twice: first proving every node's kind has a Fields row (so a new untaught primitive fails loudly), then checking each recognized node's fields against its declared value or structural slot.

nodes.name: verify!
nodes.summary: The entry point: two ordered walks over the whole program, the drift backstop first so an unrecognized node can never slip through as fine, then the per-node well-formedness check.

nodes.name: check_field
nodes.summary: Checks one operand against its declared slot, raising InvariantError either for a field the schema does not know about or for a value that does not match the slot's type.

nodes.name: check_children_are_statements
nodes.summary: Enforces the structural split: statements nest as children and value nodes live in #attrs, so a value node found among the children means a verb wired an operand as a statement.

nodes.name: list.rb
nodes.summary: The List handle a game author gets back from `list :name, capacity: N` — a bounded, ordered collection whose length changes as the game runs. The collection peer of Value: mutations record IR statements, reads hand back Values that flow into the expression DSL.
nodes.languageNotes: Its `holds: 0.0` option declares fractional items once on the list, so every read carries the scale and the author never picks or carries a fixed-point scale by hand.

nodes.name: List
nodes.summary: Ruby-array-shaped handle over a run-time list: push/<</pop/shift/[]= record statements at the current build point, while []/length/first/last/each hand back Values. Carries the list's fraction scale and the two error sentences for a mismatched number.

nodes.name: each
nodes.summary: Runs the block once per item front to back. Sugar over Builder#repeat whose count is the list's CURRENT length, so the loop tracks the list even as earlier iterations change it.

nodes.name: mixing
nodes.summary: Builds the friendly plain-language error for putting a fractional number into a whole-number list or the reverse, worded for a list (which has no left and right side the way an operator does).

nodes.name: music.rb
nodes.summary: The build-time music DSL: note frequencies, duration maths, and the song/voice contexts that turn written notes into the resolved score (frame/frequency pairs) every backend replays. Supports a single line of notes or a melody layered over a bass.
nodes.languageNotes: MAX_VOICES counts musical PARTS, not hardware channels — the writer never names a channel, the framework assigns them.

nodes.name: Music
nodes.summary: Namespace holding the C2-to-C6 note frequency table, the duration multipliers relative to a quarter note, the two-part voice budget, and the two context classes the song block is evaluated against.

nodes.name: Music::VoiceContext
nodes.summary: One part of a song: a single line of notes and rests with its own duty (tone) and volume, accumulating [frame_offset, freq_hz] events against the song's shared tempo so every part advances together.

nodes.name: Music::SongContext
nodes.summary: A song: a shared tempo plus one or more parts. Loose notes form one default part; `voice` blocks layer parts. Refuses mixing the two forms and enforces the two-part budget, and loops at the length of its longest part.

nodes.name: resolve_pitch
nodes.summary: Turns a note name (:C4, :Fs4) or a raw positive Hz value into a frequency, raising a friendly error that lists known notes for anything else.

nodes.name: duration_frames
nodes.summary: Converts a duration name (:quarter, :eighth) into a whole number of frames using the song's live tempo, so a note's length follows any tempo change.

nodes.name: voice
nodes.summary: Adds a named part played alongside the others by instance-evaluating the block against a fresh VoiceContext, then re-checks the two-part budget. Refuses to run once loose notes made a default part.

nodes.name: pager.rb
nodes.summary: Shows long CLI output a screenful at a time the way git and man do, or prints it straight through when there is nothing to page onto. The `ruby-gba build --format=ir` output, which can run to hundreds of lines, is today's one caller.
nodes.languageNotes: The subprocess runner is injected as a plain dependency so a test can assert what WOULD have run without a real `less` or a real terminal.

nodes.name: Pager
nodes.summary: Pipes text through $PAGER (falling back to `less` when it is on PATH) for an interactive terminal, and writes it unpaged everywhere else so a piped or captured build gets the whole thing.

nodes.name: page
nodes.summary: Prints text through the pager when the output stream is an interactive terminal, otherwise straight through unpaged.

nodes.name: shell_out
nodes.summary: The default runner: pipes the text into a real subprocess, falling back to printing straight through when there is no pager to run or the reader quit early (ENOENT / EPIPE).

nodes.name: pixel_bounds.rb
nodes.summary: Makes a sprite's `overlaps?` shape-accurate: on top of the plain box test from Bounds it adds a per-pixel test when both sides are sprites still colliding per-pixel. The box test gates it, so far-apart pairs never reach the expensive walk.
nodes.languageNotes: A Ruby mixin that overrides via `super`, so it composes onto Bounds rather than restating the box test — and a Box or an opted-out sprite falls back to the plain rectangle unchanged.

nodes.name: PixelBounds
nodes.summary: Mixin that ANDs a pixels_overlap IR condition onto the inherited box overlap, passing each side's pose set, current pose and position so the test follows whichever animation frame is showing.

nodes.name: overlaps?
nodes.summary: Returns the box overlap alone unless both things are per-pixel sprites, in which case it ANDs a pixels_overlap condition built from both sides' poses and positions.

nodes.name: plain_words.rb
nodes.summary: The one place holding the English name for a thing several parts of a build have to mention — the console's quick memory, the routines nobody wrote, the verbs whose node kind is not what the author typed — so three corners of the framework cannot drift into three names for one thing.
nodes.languageNotes: NOT_CALLED holds the forbidden spellings (IWRAM, fast RAM) as regexes so a test can fail when one turns up in something a build prints; code comments are exempt on purpose.

nodes.name: PlainWords
nodes.summary: Module of shared nouns: the quick-memory name and its banned synonyms, the framework-generated routine names (the game loop, the interrupt answerer, the divide routines, the mixer), and the author-facing verb for a node kind.

nodes.name: routine
nodes.summary: Names a routine for a reader: a known framework-generated one gets its plain-English name, a per-font digit routine is described in terms of the draw_number the author wrote, and anything else comes back as `func :name`.

nodes.name: pool.rb
nodes.summary: The Pool handle a game author gets from `pool :bullet, x:, y:, capacity: 64` — many instances of a component with named fields that behave. Desugars onto parallel Lists plus an active column and a free stack, so fields can never desync and every backend runs it.
nodes.languageNotes: Spawn and remove are O(1) by popping or pushing a free-slot index, so a live instance keeps a stable slot and removing one mid-iteration is just clearing a flag.

nodes.name: Pool
nodes.summary: Owns a pool's backing storage names, its spawn policy (:drop or :recycle_oldest), its per-slot pose bookkeeping for pools that face or animate, its optional tile-collision background, and the fraction scale of each field.

nodes.name: Pool::Instance
nodes.summary: One live instance as the `each` block sees it: a row handle whose fields are reached by name via method_missing, which can retire itself, hands back its slot as a Value, and gains overlaps?/edge tests/clamp_to_screen from Bounds when the pool has an image.

nodes.name: pose_node
nodes.summary: Which picture one slot shows, as a value node: a plain pool's single picture, the slot's facing, its animation frame, or the two composed as direction * frames-per-direction + frame.

nodes.name: spawn
nodes.summary: Creates a live instance, rejecting an unknown field name with a friendly error and then dispatching to the :drop or :recycle_oldest policy. All fields are set together so a half-populated instance is impossible.

nodes.name: each
nodes.summary: Walks all capacity slots and runs the block once per LIVE instance. Records the live-check through the builder rather than `.then` so the guard can carry the walk-every-slot/body-only-for-live hint without exposing it on any user `.then`.

nodes.name: spawn_recycling
nodes.summary: The :recycle_oldest policy: take a free slot when there is one, else reuse the longest-lived instance's, then write the new fields, reset the pose and stamp a fresh spawn-order age so the next full spawn can find the oldest again.

nodes.name: move
nodes.summary: Moves one instance either by a named direction or a raw (dx, dy), checking each axis on its own so it slides along a wall it is pressed against, and turning it to face the way it moved when the pool has facing pictures.

nodes.name: can_move?
nodes.summary: Whether this instance could step the given distance without meeting a solid tile, as a Condition to branch on. Raises a friendly error when the pool was never told `blocked_by` a background.

nodes.name: clear_of_tiles
nodes.summary: Sets up and calls the ONE shared tile-collision routine (the same copy a hand-declared sprite of the same size uses), then reads its clear flag back as a Condition.

nodes.name: profiler.rb
nodes.summary: Measures where a finished cartridge's frames actually went by running it on the emulator, sampling the program counter, and mapping addresses back onto the routines the build recorded. Nothing is predicted — the numbers are counts of what happened.
nodes.languageNotes: The two halves it needs come from places neither can supply the other: the emulator knows where the console was, the build knows where each routine ended up (and a routine copied into quick memory at boot runs nowhere near where it sits in the ROM).

nodes.name: Profiler
nodes.summary: Drives a measured run and renders it: routine shares, frame rate, idle share, timer tick shortfalls, whether the picture tore, and whether a tear-free screen is losing half its drawing. Also surveys every scene so a build can choose what goes in quick memory by measurement.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: The entry point: writes the ROM to a temp file, opens an emulator probe, and measures it either from a saved state, pinned to a scene, or as it plainly boots — then optionally reads the screen for tearing and flicker.

nodes.name: tearing_in
nodes.summary: Did the picture actually tear — the question the build can only ask, not answer. Steps a handful of frames and reads each, because a tearing game tears steadily and reading a frame costs a bus read per pixel.

nodes.name: check_state_matches!
nodes.summary: Refuses a save state taken from a different BUILD of the same game by comparing the cartridge CRC32 the state records. The emulator only catches a different game, so reading a stale state would measure the wrong code while still looking like numbers.

nodes.name: scene_state
nodes.summary: Finds where a named scene's selector variable lives and what value means that scene, with friendly errors for a game with no scenes, an unknown scene name, or a selector this cannot reach.

nodes.name: pinned_to
nodes.summary: Holds the game in one scene and measures it by writing the scene variable before EVERY frame — writing it once is not enough, because a game left to itself leaves the scene within a few frames and the wrong routines get measured under its name.

nodes.name: every_scene
nodes.summary: Measures the whole game one scene at a time and combines each routine's cost by taking the LARGEST, not the average — a routine carrying one scene has earned quick memory whatever it does in the others.

nodes.name: build_result
