nodes.summary: Assembles the finished Result: routine lines sorted dearest-first with their plain-English labels and which memory they ran from, plus separate lines for what ran outside every known routine.

nodes.name: progress.rb
nodes.summary: What a build says it is doing while it does it, so a slow build is distinguishable from a hung one. Deliberately an object rather than a stream plus a flag, with a do-nothing default so no caller ever has to check whether anybody is listening.
nodes.languageNotes: No percentage anywhere, on purpose: two build phases have no bound, so a denominator would have to be invented and an invented one gets believed. Elapsed time per phase instead.

nodes.name: Progress
nodes.summary: The silent default: step / of / tick / done all present and all no-ops, plus the factories for the shared silent instance and a stream-writing one.

nodes.name: Progress::Printed
nodes.summary: Writes progress to a stream, keeping one rewritten line on a terminal and one line per finished phase everywhere else, so a test sees one tidy line per phase. Ticks are counted and the clock consulted only every 256 of them.

nodes.name: step
nodes.summary: Begins a named phase: finishes and writes out whatever was running first (so an elapsed time is only reported once it really has elapsed), resets the counters, then draws and starts the refresher thread on a terminal.

nodes.name: keep_awake
nodes.summary: A small thread that keeps the elapsed time climbing while a phase is open, because a phase can spend fifteen seconds inside ONE call and a line only redrawn when told would sit at 0.0s and read as a hang. Waits on a condition variable so closing a phase ends it at once.

nodes.name: rom.rb
nodes.summary: Manages the raw cartridge byte buffer and writes the GBA header — Nintendo logo, title, codes, fixed byte, entry branch, complement checksum, power-of-two padding — then validates the finished image. The counterpart to a backend's lowering.
nodes.languageNotes: Every header offset comes from Constants rather than a magic number, and the logo sits outside the checksum range so writing it cannot disturb the checksum computed later.

nodes.name: ROM
nodes.summary: The finished cartridge: a byte buffer plus the optional BuildRecord that lets it report on itself (source program, routine placement, variable addresses, palette entries, compression). Exposes #write, #size and the user-facing #profile.

nodes.name: assemble
nodes.summary: Packages finished machine code into a cartridge: build the header, drop the code in after it, and finalize. Carries the build record through so the finished ROM can report on itself.

nodes.name: finalize!
nodes.summary: Writes the entry branch at 0x00, computes and stores the header complement checksum, pads the image up to the next power of two the way real cartridges are sized, and runs ROMValidator unless asked not to.

nodes.name: profile
nodes.summary: The author-facing measurement verb: runs the cartridge and prints (or emits as JSON) what the build made of the game and where its frames actually went. Takes `scene:` to hold the game in one screen or `from:` to measure a saved moment.

nodes.name: rom_validator.rb
nodes.summary: Validates a finished ROM image for the structural problems that make the BIOS or an accurate emulator reject it: too small, a wrong fixed byte or Nintendo logo, a bad header checksum, an entry branch that misses the code, no code at all, an empty title.
nodes.languageNotes: Deliberately post-lowering and distinct from the IR guardrails, which reason about the program before any bytes exist. An error means the ROM will not run; a warning means it runs but something is off.

nodes.name: ROMValidator
nodes.summary: Runs seven structural checks over the raw cartridge bytes and returns a Result of errors and warnings that can report itself as text. Checks a ROM object or a .gba file on disk.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: Runs every structural check in order — size, fixed byte, logo, checksum, entry branch, code region, title — and packages the accumulated errors and warnings into a Result.

nodes.name: check_entry_branch
nodes.summary: Decodes the word at 0x00 as an unconditional ARM branch and sign-extends its offset, then reports a friendly error if the target lands inside the header or past the end of the ROM.

nodes.name: roomy_memory.rb
nodes.summary: The value object reporting what fell into the console's larger, slower work memory — a decision nobody wrote and nothing else can show. It matters twice: a game that used to fail to build now builds, and a big cold collection left in quick memory would push hot code out to the cartridge.

nodes.name: RoomyMemory
nodes.summary: A Data.define of used bytes, free bytes and the named collections that landed there, with #total and a #to_h for the JSON profile.

nodes.name: routine_profile.rb
nodes.summary: Persists what a game's frames were measured to spend per routine, so a later build can read it back and place the right routines in quick memory. The build's one decision it cannot measure its way to — measure once, feed it back, and the second build is right by measurement.
nodes.languageNotes: Keyed by ROUTINE NAME, not address, which is what makes it survive a rebuild — addresses all move when a program changes, a name only changes when somebody renames it.

nodes.name: RoutineProfile
nodes.summary: Reads and writes the saved profile JSON, ranks routines by measured instructions-a-frame, reports routines the program no longer has, and answers whether one does enough work to be worth the room (WORTH_MOVING).

nodes.name: read
nodes.summary: Loads a saved profile, returning nil for a missing file (the ordinary case on a first build, not an error) and raising a friendly ProfileError telling the author to measure again when the JSON is unreadable.

nodes.name: sample.rb
nodes.summary: The Sample handle a game author gets from `sample :boom, pcm: [...]` — a recorded clip played through the sampled-audio hardware rather than a synthesized PSG tone. The framework hides the sound FIFO, the DMA that feeds it and the playback-rate timer.

nodes.name: Sample
nodes.summary: Records play and stop statements for an embedded clip, validating the volume level and any pitch note against the framework's note table, and supporting one-shot, seamless-loop and pitch-shifted playback.

nodes.name: validate_note!
nodes.summary: Checks a note name is one the framework knows, with a friendly error naming the supported range. Shared by `sample note:` and `play pitch:` so both say the same thing.

nodes.name: play
nodes.summary: Records a play_sample statement after validating the volume level and any pitch. Plays once at full volume by default; `loop: true` makes it seamless background music and `pitch:` reads through the clip faster or slower.

nodes.name: scale.rb
nodes.summary: The one copy of the rules for bringing a number onto the same footing as the place it is going — whole numbers or numbers carrying a fraction. Shared by variables, lists, pool fields and expressions, each supplying only its own two error sentences.
nodes.languageNotes: Deliberately not a method on Value: the three non-Value places used to build a throwaway Value to borrow these rules, which was indistinguishable from an author's dropped expression to the orphaned-expression guardrail.

nodes.name: Scale
nodes.summary: Holds how many fraction bits a place keeps plus two message callbacks, and answers #node_matching / #operand_matching — converting a literal for free, refusing a run-time number of the wrong kind, and refusing two different fraction scales.

nodes.name: node_matching
nodes.summary: The core rule: a whole number WRITTEN in the program is converted (because `speed + 1` plainly means one faster), but a number the game works out cannot be, since nothing can tell whether a counter holding 3 means three or three sixty-fourths.

nodes.name: sound.rb
nodes.summary: The shared meaning of the sound ops in two layers: a hardware-free musical layer (sound and noise presets, wavetable shapes) every backend agrees on, and a Registers submodule encoding those musical values into the console's exact sound-register writes.
nodes.languageNotes: The wavetable is written to BOTH wave-RAM banks, sidestepping the classic silence bug where you upload to the bank the channel is not currently looping.

nodes.name: Sound
nodes.summary: The musical layer: built-in beep and noise presets as plain values, the resolution rules that apply a caller's overrides, and the four built-in wave shapes as 32 four-bit samples — all with no hardware in sight, so a headless interpreter can use them.

nodes.name: Sound::Registers
nodes.summary: The console-specific half: each method returns the [register_address, 16-bit value] pairs a backend just stores, for enabling sound, a channel-2 effect, a sustaining music note on channel 1 or 2, a channel-4 noise hit, and the channel-3 wavetable.

nodes.name: resolve_effect
nodes.summary: Resolves a beep into concrete musical values: a preset name looked up first among the program's own defined sounds then the built-ins, or a raw frequency in Hz, with any non-nil override replacing the base value.

nodes.name: wavetable
nodes.summary: Generates the 32 four-bit samples for a named wave shape — square, sawtooth, triangle or sine — so both backends agree on the timbre and a game only ever says `wave :triangle`.

nodes.name: wave_play
nodes.summary: Builds the register writes to play a wavetable on channel 3, uploading the same table to both wave-RAM banks so whichever the channel loops is the wanted waveform, then setting the level and the restart-plus-rate word.

nodes.name: sprite.rb
nodes.summary: The software (save-under) Sprite handle for bitmap screens: a named image with a position it owns that moves leaving no trail, because it remembers the pixels underneath itself and paints them back before drawing at the new spot.
nodes.languageNotes: The per-frame repaint is two passes over all sprites — every one erased, then every one drawn — which is what lets sprites overlap cleanly, since no sprite can capture a neighbour that has not been erased yet.

nodes.name: Sprite
nodes.summary: Exposes x/y as Values and the move/move_to/clamp_to_screen/center_on_screen/face/play/hide/show vocabulary, plus the two IR nodes the per-frame repaint uses. Turning and resizing raise friendly errors pointing at screen :tiled.

nodes.name: pose_index_node
nodes.summary: Which pose to show right now as a value node: 0 for a plain sprite, the facing or frame selector, the two composed for a directional animation, or the current Aseprite clip's offset plus its frame.

nodes.name: move
nodes.summary: Moves the sprite either by a named direction (including diagonals, with `by:` for speed) or a raw dx/dy nudge, and turns a posed sprite to face the way it moved when it has a pose for that direction.

nodes.name: face
nodes.summary: Swaps the sprite to a direction's pose in place with no move, raising friendly errors for a sprite given no `facing:` poses and for a direction it has no pose for.

nodes.name: draw_at_current
nodes.summary: The save-under core: capture what is under the current spot, draw the sprite there, and record that spot as where it was last drawn so the next frame's erase targets it.

nodes.name: table.rb
nodes.summary: The Table handle for a read-only ROM lookup declared with `table` — indexed at run time by a Value, with a build-time fixed size. Reads compose with the expression DSL, so `sin[angle]` drops straight into `y.set sin[angle]`.
nodes.languageNotes: An out-of-range index is made safe by the read itself: a power-of-two table wraps, any other size clamps to the ends — and a table written with Floats hands back values carrying a fraction.

nodes.name: Table
nodes.summary: Wraps a named ROM table: `[]` builds a table_get value node at a run-time index and returns it as a Value carrying the table's fraction scale, while `length` is a plain build-time Integer.

nodes.name: tearing.rb
nodes.summary: Measures whether a built cartridge actually tore on a real emulator run: it compares the picture the display put on screen row by row against the picture sitting in video memory at the frame boundary, and every differing row is one the display showed before the game had finished painting it. Deliberately a measurement rather than an estimate, because tearing is a race down the screen that a total-work estimate cannot decide.
nodes.languageNotes: Ruby `module_function` module plus a `Data.define` reading; `Reading.none` encodes "not measured here" so a screen mode with no framebuffer can never be misread as "no tear".

nodes.name: RubyGBA::Tearing
nodes.summary: Module holding the tear measurement: constants for where a direct-color framebuffer lives, a gate saying whether this program's screen mode can be measured at all, and the row-by-row comparison itself.

nodes.name: Tearing::Reading
nodes.summary: Immutable result of one tear measurement: how many visible rows went up stale, and where the seam ran. `Reading.none` plus `measured?` keep "we did not look" distinct from "nothing was wrong".

nodes.name: measurable?
nodes.summary: Whether a tear can be measured for this program at all — it needs exactly one framebuffer, so buffered, tiled and affine screen modes are all excluded.

nodes.name: read
nodes.summary: Reads one frame of an emulator probe stopped at a frame boundary and returns a Reading: the rows where what the display showed differs from what the game had finished drawing.

nodes.name: shown_rows
nodes.summary: Unpacks the emulator's 8-bit-per-channel frame buffer back into the 15-bit colors the program actually wrote, grouped one array per screen row — the picture the display really put up.

nodes.name: drawn_rows
nodes.summary: Reads the framebuffer straight out of the console's video memory, one row at a time — the picture the game meant to show, which is the reference the shown picture is compared against.

nodes.name: test_patterns.rb
nodes.summary: Built-in diagnostic ROM generators that build unmistakable patterns (solid fill, color bars, corner markers, crosshair) through the DSL. If these do not appear in an emulator, the problem is the emulator setup rather than the user's program.

nodes.name: RubyGBA::TestPatterns
nodes.summary: Module of four tiny self-contained programs, each built through the public DSL and returned as a finished ROM, for sanity-checking a rendering pipeline end to end.

nodes.name: solid_fill
nodes.summary: Builds a ROM that fills the whole 240x160 bitmap screen with one color — the most basic check that anything renders at all.

nodes.name: color_bars
nodes.summary: Builds a ROM with three 80-pixel vertical stripes (red, green, blue) to prove each color channel renders independently.

nodes.name: corners
nodes.summary: Builds a ROM with a differently colored 20x20 square in each screen corner, checking that pixel addressing is right at the screen boundaries.

nodes.name: crosshair
nodes.summary: Builds a ROM drawing horizontal and vertical lines through the screen center plus a center dot, so the coordinate system's origin and orientation can be read off the picture.

nodes.name: tick_rate.rb
nodes.summary: Counts what rate a hardware timer really delivered on a real run, by counting how many times its handler's first instruction actually executed and holding that against elapsed hardware frames. Exists because timer ticks have no queue: a handler that overruns silently loses ticks and nothing on screen says so.
nodes.languageNotes: Documents at length why it reports a number and never warns: drawing stalls interrupts too, so the share lost to a slow handler and the share lost to ordinary `clear_screen` calls overlap completely and no threshold can separate them.

nodes.name: RubyGBA::TickRate
nodes.summary: Module turning a tick count and a run duration into a per-timer rate reading, with thresholds for what is worth printing and how many ticks a window must expect before the ratio means anything.

nodes.name: TickRate::Reading
nodes.summary: Immutable per-timer result holding the rate asked for and the rate that arrived, with `share` as the fraction delivered and `short?` flagging a gap big enough to change what the game does.

nodes.name: read
nodes.summary: Turns one timer's answered-tick count and the run's real duration into a Reading, returning an unmeasured reading when too few ticks were expected for the ratio to be anything but noise.

nodes.name: timer.rb
nodes.summary: The user-facing handle a `timer :name, per_second: N` verb hands back: reading its tick count as a Value, registering a per-tick handler, and stopping it. The hardware prescaler, reload and count-reading are managed by the framework behind this surface.

nodes.name: RubyGBA::Timer
nodes.summary: A handle to one hardware timer. Each method records an IR node into the build rather than doing anything itself, and the chainable methods return self.

nodes.name: ticks
nodes.summary: Hands back the timer's overflow count wrapped as a Value, so it reads and compares like any other variable in the expression DSL.

nodes.name: on_tick
nodes.summary: Records a block to run on every timer overflow, driven by the timer's own interrupt rather than the frame loop — the low-level seam that metronomes, sampled-audio playback and music timing sit on.

nodes.name: value.rb
nodes.summary: The expression DSL's central handle: a variable, literal or arithmetic expression that ordinary Ruby operators build bigger IR nodes out of, with comparisons producing a Condition rather than a Ruby boolean. Also the one coercion boundary through which every operand reaches the IR, and the home of the fixed-point scale rules.
nodes.languageNotes: Deliberately implements no `<=>`/Comparable — that would hand back build-time booleans and revive the `if (x > 5)` footgun `.then` exists to stop. It also overrides `then`, `to_int` and `coerce` purely to turn Ruby's own behaviour into plain-language teaching errors.

nodes.name: RubyGBA::Value
nodes.summary: Wraps one IR value node and overloads Ruby's arithmetic, bitwise, shift and comparison operators to build bigger nodes; mutators (set/add/sub/clamp/approach/flip) record statements, and mutating an expression that names no variable is a friendly error.

nodes.name: self.node_for
nodes.summary: The single coercion boundary: turns any operand (a Value, an Integer, a Symbol, a raw node) into an IR value node, so nothing but a value node ever reaches the IR and a Value and its `:symbol` stay interchangeable everywhere.

nodes.name: self.fixed_number
nodes.summary: Returns the number an operand already has, or nil when the game works it out at run time — asking for the answer rather than the Ruby class, because a bare Integer, a wrapped literal and a handle standing for one are all the same fact.

nodes.name: initialize
nodes.summary: Builds a handle over an IR node with an optional variable name and fixed-point scale; only an expression (not a named handle) pays for the stack walk that pins the author's source line for the orphaned-expression guardrail.

Multiplication that decides for the author which multiply is the dangerous one: times a plain count is ordinary, times another fixed-point value is widened to full width automatically so the doubly-scaled intermediate cannot overflow.

Division, the mirror of the fixed-point multiply: dividing one fractional value by another widens the numerator first so the answer keeps its fraction, and saturates rather than wrapping when the result will not fit.
Remainder following Ruby's own sign convention (so -1 % 64 is 63), which is what an angle stepping below zero or a map coordinate off the left edge wants.

nodes.name: then
nodes.summary: Overrides Ruby's universal `then` to raise a teaching error: branching on a bare number (the C habit `if (flags & MASK)`) would run the block at build time and record its body with no test around it.

nodes.name: to_int
nodes.summary: Replaces Ruby's opaque "no implicit conversion" message with a plain-language one naming the real case — a runtime value on the right of `<<` or `>>` — and pointing at the rewrite that works.

nodes.name: coerce
nodes.summary: Lets a plain number stand on the left of an operator (`160 / distance`, the perspective divide), giving the literal this value's own fixed-point scale so the answer keeps its fraction.

nodes.name: to_i
nodes.summary: Drops the fraction with an arithmetic shift (rounding down, so -0.5 becomes -1) — one instruction rather than the divide it replaces, and a no-op on a value that is already whole.

nodes.name: times_fraction
nodes.summary: Explicit full-width multiply of two values carrying the same number of fraction bits, the escape hatch below the automatic handling in `*`. Its comment records why the scale does not travel with the value yet.

nodes.name: shift_count!
nodes.summary: Validates a shift count: a written-down count that would empty the number is a friendly error, a negative count clears rather than reversing direction, and a runtime count is clamped instead of rejected because it comes out of data.

nodes.name: verifier.rb
nodes.summary: Runs a finished ROM headlessly in mGBA and reads back real rendered pixels, real audio samples and real IWRAM variable values — the definitive answer to "did my ROM actually draw anything?" that the emulator-backed tests assert against.
nodes.languageNotes: Save files are collected in one process-wide temp directory removed via `at_exit`, because a Verifier still alive at process exit is never garbage-collected and a per-object cleanup would strand exactly those.

nodes.name: RubyGBA::Verifier
nodes.summary: Lazily renders a ROM for N frames with optional held input, then exposes pixel reads, region assertions, raw memory reads, variable reads, audio energy, an ASCII screen map and a summary report over the captured state.

nodes.name: initialize
nodes.summary: Stores the ROM, frame count, per-frame held-key source and the backend's variable-address map, then loads the emulator immediately so a missing native build fails fast rather than at first pixel read.

nodes.name: pixel
nodes.summary: Reads the 8-bit RGB color at a screen coordinate out of the emulator's captured frame, unpacking mGBA's native XBGR8 byte order.

nodes.name: pixel_gba
nodes.summary: The same pixel as a 15-bit BGR555 value — the number the program itself wrote — so an assertion can compare against a color the DSL produced rather than against emulator channel widths.

nodes.name: frame_gba
nodes.summary: The whole captured frame converted to 15-bit console colors in one pass, for callers comparing a full screen rather than sampling points.

nodes.name: region_mismatch
nodes.summary: Finds the first pixel in a rectangle that is not the expected color and reports where and what it was — the diagnostic half of `region_color?`, so a failing assertion says which pixel disagreed.

nodes.name: var
nodes.summary: Reads a DSL variable's value back out of IWRAM after the run, using the name-to-address map the lowering backend produced — how a test asserts on computed state rather than on pixels.

nodes.name: audio_energy
nodes.summary: Sums the absolute amplitude of every PCM sample the run produced — a deliberately crude "did any sound come out?" measure that ignores pitch and waveform.

nodes.name: audio_energy_by_frame
nodes.summary: The same energy figure per displayed frame, which is what reveals sound arriving in bursts with holes between them — a defect the run's total energy cannot show.

nodes.name: screen_map
nodes.summary: Renders the screen as a character grid, one character per 8x8 tile sampled at its center — a human-readable dump of what is on screen for debugging a failing verification.

nodes.name: report
nodes.summary: A text summary of the rendered frame: frames run, how many distinct colors appeared, the ten most common with their pixel shares, and the ASCII screen map.

nodes.name: ensure_rendered!
nodes.summary: The lazy render: writes the ROM to a temp file, opens it in the emulator with a shared save directory, runs the requested frames feeding held keys per frame, and captures the final frame's pixels plus every frame's audio chunk.

nodes.name: version.rb
nodes.summary: Declares the gem's version constant, read by the gemspec so packaging and the library agree on one number.

nodes.name: video_memory.rb
nodes.summary: The value objects the build report uses to say how much of the console's fixed picture memory the sprites and tiles took, how much is left, and how much room the framework's own silent choices bought back — half-size storage for low-color art, shared identical pictures, reused pose pieces. None of that survives into a running cartridge, so the build is the only place it can be seen.
nodes.languageNotes: A `Data.define` reopened as a `class` so nested Data types (Area, Objects) can live under the same name; each defines a keyword-only `initialize` override purely to give defaults.

nodes.name: RubyGBA::VideoMemory
nodes.summary: Top-level picture-memory report holding the two areas (sprites and background tiles) and the sprite-object count, with `any?` saying whether anything was measured and `to_h` producing the JSON shape.

nodes.name: VideoMemory::Area
nodes.summary: One memory area's accounting: bytes used against capacity, how many pictures took small versus big storage, what the small ones saved, how many were shared outright, bytes not paid for because a pose piece was already there, and bytes skipped to align a layer's tile base.

nodes.name: VideoMemory::Objects
nodes.summary: How many of the console's 128 sprite objects the game spends, which is not the number of sprites the author declared: a picture bigger than the largest hardware sprite costs several, and a placed fade shadows each kept sprite object for object.

nodes.name: wav.rb
nodes.summary: Loads a .wav file into the 8-bit signed mono PCM the sampled-audio hardware plays, walking the RIFF container to find the fmt and data chunks and converting 8- or 16-bit, mono or stereo audio down to one channel while keeping the file's own sample rate.
nodes.languageNotes: Every failure path raises a Wav::Error whose message says what was wrong and what to export instead, rather than letting a malformed unpack produce silent garbage.

nodes.name: RubyGBA::Wav
nodes.summary: Module-function WAV reader plus its Error class and the PCM format code, exposing a load-from-path and a parse-from-bytes entry point that both return { bytes:, rate: }.

nodes.name: load
nodes.summary: Reads a .wav file from disk in binary mode and hands its bytes to the parser, naming the path in any error raised.

nodes.name: parse
nodes.summary: Validates the RIFF/WAVE header, locates the fmt and data chunks, rejects anything but uncompressed PCM with a plain-language error, and returns the converted mono bytes alongside the file's sample rate.

nodes.name: find_chunk
nodes.summary: Walks the RIFF chunk list from the fixed 12-byte offset, honoring each chunk's little-endian size and even-length padding, and returns the bytes of the first chunk with the wanted id.

nodes.name: to_signed_8bit_mono
nodes.summary: Converts raw sample bytes to one channel of 8-bit signed PCM: recentering unsigned 8-bit samples, keeping the signed high byte of 16-bit ones, and averaging interleaved channels down to mono.

nodes.name: whole.rb
nodes.summary: One place to ask whether an author-written argument is a valid whole number — a capacity, a rate, a size, a digit count. It only answers; each of the fifteen callers still raises its own error, because each has something different to teach.

nodes.name: RubyGBA::Whole
nodes.summary: Two module-function predicates: `positive?` for a count there must be at least one of, and `within?` for a whole number inside a caller-named range.

nodes.name: ruby-gba.gemspec
nodes.summary: The gem packaging manifest: names the library, reads its version constant from lib/ruby_gba/version.rb, ships lib/test/bin plus the Rakefile, exposes the `ruby-gba` executable, and declares Thor as the one runtime dependency (rake, minitest and simplecov for development).

nodes.name: emitted.rb
nodes.summary: The `rake emitted` driver: builds every example twice — once against the working tree's library, once against the library restored from another commit — and reports what moved. Reports three independent numbers (emitted instructions, embedded asset bytes, estimated per-frame work) because a change to the lowering and a change to the assets move different ones.
nodes.languageNotes: The other version of the library is obtained with `git archive | tar -x` into a tmpdir rather than a checkout, deliberately: a checkout would bring that commit's examples along too, and an edited game would then score as a compiler change.

nodes.name: Emitted
nodes.summary: Top-level module for the emitted-code comparison: the quiet-noise floors, the two value objects, the driving functions that fan out to child probe processes, and the two reporters.

nodes.name: Emitted::Measurement
nodes.summary: What one example emitted against one version of the library: code bytes, data bytes, frame estimate, a per-kind shape count of the program that was built, an optional byte breakdown, or an error when it would not build at all.

nodes.name: Emitted::Row
nodes.summary: One example measured on both sides, computing each delta and classifying the result as same, quiet, changed, new, broken or failing. `same_program?` compares the two shape counts so a library that now builds a different program from the same example is flagged rather than silently measured as a lowering change.

nodes.name: Emitted::Drilldown
nodes.summary: For a run narrowed to one example, renders where that program's bytes moved along three axes — by kind of operation, by func, by line of the game's own source — with a collapsed tail and a line naming what was emitted outside any statement.

nodes.name: Emitted::Report
nodes.summary: Turns the paired measurements into the printed output: broken examples first, the caveat about examples that built a different program, the delta table, the optional drilldown, the tally of rows below the noise floor, and the one summary line worth keeping.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: The entry point: resolves the reference commit, measures every selected example against the working tree and against that commit's library, and renders the report. The byte drilldown is enabled only when the run is narrowed to one example.

nodes.name: examples
nodes.summary: Finds the example programs to measure — files under examples/ that declare a game, optionally filtered by a comma-separated ONLY list — so helper and multi-file parts are reached by their owner rather than measured on their own.

nodes.name: measure
nodes.summary: Builds every example against one copy of the library, one child process each, returning a name-to-Measurement map.

nodes.name: probe
nodes.summary: Spawns emitted_probe.rb for one example against one library root and captures its JSON line — a separate process so the two library versions never meet and one exploding example cannot take the run down.

nodes.name: measurement
nodes.summary: Parses the child's last stdout line as the report, falling back to a Measurement carrying whatever the dying process managed to say on stderr — being unbuildable is a result to report, not a reason to stop.

nodes.name: with_lib_at
nodes.summary: Lays only lib/ as it was at a commit into a temporary directory via `git archive` piped to `tar`, yields its path, and cleans up — deliberately leaving the working tree's examples in place so the pairing measures the compiler and not the game.

nodes.name: emitted_attribution.rb
nodes.summary: Attributes emitted bytes to the part of the program that produced them — per func, per kind of operation, per line of the game's own source. Counts bytes per kind rather than nodes per kind, because both sides build the same tree and only the bytes each node turns into move; counting nodes would report "no change" for exactly the changes this explains.
nodes.languageNotes: Bytes are attributed exclusively via a depth stack, so a loop is charged for its own bookkeeping and not its body and the columns add up instead of double-counting at every level of nesting.

nodes.name: EmittedAttribution
nodes.summary: Module that either asks a modern library for its own attribution table or watches an older one being lowered, then reduces whichever it got to the same three maps plus the unattributed remainder.

nodes.name: EmittedAttribution::Recorder
nodes.summary: Prepended to a throwaway backend subclass, it wraps the lowering's single statement method with a singleton override that records how many bytes each statement produced on its own, keeping a depth stack so nested statements are not counted twice.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses `prepend` on an anonymous subclass plus `define_singleton_method` on the backend's own Lowering instance, so the process measuring one build is not changed for everything else it does.

nodes.name: recording
nodes.summary: Returns the plain backend class when that library already counts its own emitted bytes, otherwise an anonymous subclass with the Recorder prepended.

nodes.name: measure
nodes.summary: Lowers a program with a backend that will report attribution and returns the full byte breakdown.

nodes.name: breakdown
nodes.summary: Builds the Breakdown: func sizes from the backend's own exact span table, bytes summed by node kind and by the source line that asked for each node (framework-made nodes grouped together), and the remainder emitted around the program — boot code, the data region, the interrupt handler — named rather than quietly missing.

nodes.name: rows_for
nodes.summary: Yields node-and-bytes pairs however this build was measured — the library's own instructions-per-node table, or the watched per-site records — so the two reduce identically.

nodes.name: sum_by
nodes.summary: Totals bytes under a caller-supplied key, drops zero rows, and sorts biggest-first with the key as a tiebreak so the output is stable between runs.

nodes.name: emitted_baseline.json
nodes.summary: The recorded code and data size of every example, checked in so `rake emitted:check` can fail on any growth. Sorted and pretty-printed on purpose: its diff is where a reviewer sees what a feature cost.

nodes.name: emitted_baseline.rb
nodes.summary: Records every example's emitted size into tools/emitted_baseline.json and fails the build if anything has grown past it. Answers the question no ad-hoc comparison can — has anything crept up since we last agreed a number — and treats any growth as a failure, because a reproducible build leaves no noise for a tolerance to absorb and a tolerance would only be a budget for creep.
nodes.languageNotes: The per-frame estimate is deliberately not recorded: its weights are re-measured from the emulator now and then, so it would churn for reasons unrelated to the emitted code this guards.

nodes.name: Emitted::Baseline
nodes.summary: The record and check halves of the baseline: measures every example against the working tree's library, reads and writes the sorted pretty-printed JSON document, and renders a Verdict.

nodes.name: Baseline::Verdict
nodes.summary: Pure comparison of recorded against measured sizes, classifying each example as grown, shrunk, unrecorded or gone and rendering the verdict with the one command that accepts new numbers. Being pure, it can be tested without building anything.

nodes.name: grew
nodes.summary: Finds every example bigger than its recorded size and renders each as a readable line, reporting code growth in instructions where the byte delta divides evenly and data growth in bytes.

nodes.name: failures
nodes.summary: Prints the failing half of a verdict — examples that would not build, examples that grew, examples missing from the baseline — and closes with the command that accepts the new numbers and the note that the resulting diff is what shows the cost.

nodes.name: record
nodes.summary: Measures every example, refuses to record anything if any of them fails to build, writes the new baseline document, and shows what changed against the previous one.

nodes.name: check
nodes.summary: Reads the recorded baseline, measures every example now, and renders the verdict — returning false (so the rake task fails) on any growth, unbuildable example or unrecorded new one.

nodes.name: read
nodes.summary: Loads the baseline JSON into a name-to-sizes map, treating a missing or malformed file as simply empty. Example names stay strings, matching what the measurement produces, so symbolising would not rename every example and make each look brand new.

nodes.name: write
nodes.summary: Writes the baseline document sorted and pretty-printed, so its diff is readable in a review — that diff being the whole reason the file is checked in.

nodes.name: emitted_probe.rb
nodes.summary: The child half of `rake emitted`: a standalone script that loads ONE example against ONE copy of the library and prints what it emitted as a line of JSON — code bytes, data bytes, a per-kind shape count of the program that was built, an optional byte breakdown, and the frame estimate. Runs in its own process so the two library versions never meet and one exploding example cannot take the run down.
nodes.languageNotes: Two deliberate tricks keep the pairing honest: the working tree's lib/ruby_gba.rb is pushed into $LOADED_FEATURES so an example's own require_relative becomes a no-op, and $stdout is swapped for a StringIO so an example that prints cannot land in the middle of the JSON. Anything the older library cannot answer is reported as nil rather than failing the run.

nodes.name: make_example_assets.rb
nodes.summary: Draws from plain pixel data the PNG art and CSV tilemap the importer examples read — a two-cell tile sheet, a four-frame walk-cycle sprite sheet on a transparent background, and a 30x20 room exported the way a map editor would. Generated rather than committed as opaque binaries, so anyone can see and change exactly what they contain and re-run the script.

nodes.name: MakeExampleAssets
nodes.summary: Module holding the ASCII room layout, the console-color palette, and the drawing routines that turn both into files under examples/assets/.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: Creates the assets directory if needed and writes the tile sheet, hero sheet and level CSV.

nodes.name: level_csv
nodes.summary: Turns the ASCII room into a CSV grid of tile numbers in the shape a map editor exports — 1 for brick, 2 for floor, 0 for empty.

nodes.name: tiles_png
nodes.summary: Builds the two-cell tile sheet as RGBA pixels — an 8x8 brick beside an 8x8 floor — by asking the per-pixel routines for each cell's color.

nodes.name: hero_png
nodes.summary: Builds the four-frame 16x16 walk sprite sheet laid out side by side on a fully transparent background, so the imported sprite is a cut-out.

nodes.name: draw_hero_frame
nodes.summary: Draws one walk-cycle frame into the sheet — body, legs swinging with the frame index, and an eye — as the per-frame difference that makes the cycle read as walking.

nodes.name: rgba_png
nodes.summary: Encodes an RGBA pixel array as a minimal PNG using Ruby's built-in zlib — header, deflated scanlines with their filter bytes, and CRC-checked chunks — so no image gem is needed.

nodes.name: make_piano_assets.rb
nodes.summary: Draws the hand sprites and synthesizes the single piano note that examples/piano.rb imports: a left and right hand in a resting pose and one pose per finger pressed, plus a ~0.6s C4 WAV the `instrument` verb pitches across the keys. Generated from plain data for the same reason as the other asset script — so the checked-in binaries are inspectable and reproducible.
nodes.languageNotes: Finger geometry is documented so the silhouette reads as a hand rather than a comb: resting lengths differ (middle longest) while a pressed finger extends to a common lower row, and the right hand is the left hand's mirrored length list.

nodes.name: MakePianoAssets
nodes.summary: Module holding the hand's geometry constants, the console-color palette, the note's rate/pitch/length, and the routines that write every pose PNG and the WAV under examples/assets/.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: Writes every asset: the right hand resting plus one pose per pressed finger, the left hand resting plus its two-finger block chord, and the piano note WAV.

nodes.name: hand_png
nodes.summary: Draws one 64x32 hand sprite on a transparent background — the shallow palm plus four fingers, each either at its resting length or stabbing down to the keys.

nodes.name: draw_finger
nodes.summary: Draws one finger down to a given tip row with its outline, the darker seam beside it and a pale nail at the tip.

nodes.name: piano_wav
nodes.summary: Synthesizes a piano-ish middle-C note as PCM samples — a decaying harmonic stack rather than a bare sine — long enough to ring under the next note.

nodes.name: wav_bytes
nodes.summary: Wraps the synthesized samples in a minimal RIFF/WAVE container — the header, fmt and data chunks the framework's own WAV loader reads back.

nodes.name: rgba_png
nodes.summary: The same minimal zlib-based PNG encoder as the other asset script, turning an RGBA pixel array into a checked-in image file with no image gem involved.

nodes.name: parallel_test.rb
nodes.summary: Shards the test suite across processes for `rake test:parallel` and renders the whole run as if it were one serial run. Both halves live here: required by the Rakefile as the parent, run as a script as the child. Children never print — each installs a minitest reporter streaming structured records back over fd 3, so the parent shows one dot stream, one numbered failure list and one summary.
nodes.languageNotes: Processes rather than threads on purpose: the emulator releases the GVL around run_frame so emulator-backed files would overlap, but IR lowering, the cost model and the assembler are pure Ruby and would still crawl. Per-file timings are cached beside the suite and smoothed, so one noisy run cannot dictate next week's split.

nodes.name: ParallelTest
nodes.summary: The parent side (sharding, spawning, pumping the pipes, reporting, maintaining the timings cache) plus the child entry point that requires only its slice and swaps minitest's reporters for the streaming one.

nodes.name: ParallelTest::ShardReporter
nodes.summary: The minitest reporter installed in each child: tallies counters, bills each test's time to the file that defined it, and emits tagged lines over the control pipe — a progress character per test, a JSON result per failure, and the final times and totals.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: The parent entry point: picks a worker count and one shared seed (so any parallel failure reproduces under a plain serial run), loads timings, shards, spawns, pumps the children to completion, saves new timings and reports.

nodes.name: shard
nodes.summary: Greedy longest-processing-time-first bin packing: walks the files heaviest to lightest, dropping each into the shard with the least work so far — the classic makespan approximation, provably within 4/3 of optimal.

nodes.name: weigher
nodes.summary: Builds the per-file weight function: file size on a cold run with no timings, otherwise the recorded time plus a measured per-process overhead, with the median standing in for a file never timed.

nodes.name: spawn_shard
nodes.summary: Spawns one child with three pipes: fd 3 carries the structured record stream, while stdout and stderr carry whatever the tests themselves printed and are kept out of the way until the end.

nodes.name: pump
nodes.summary: One IO.select loop over every child's two pipes: progress characters are echoed live so the dot stream reads like a single run, stray output is buffered, and a control pipe hitting EOF is the one moment a child's wall time can be measured.

nodes.name: consume_records
nodes.summary: Splits the control buffer into whole lines and dispatches by tag — P for a progress character, R for a JSON result, T for per-file times, Z for the shard's tallies — leaving any partial line in the buffer.

nodes.name: report
nodes.summary: Renders the single unified summary: renumbered failures, merged counters, elapsed time across processes, the slowest files, stray child output, and an abort naming the failing shards with the command to reproduce them serially at the same seed.

nodes.name: report_slowest
nodes.summary: Always prints where the time went, and says when one file alone sets a floor the worker count cannot get under — once packing is driven by real numbers, the single slowest file becomes what decides run length, and that is invisible unless printed.

nodes.name: report_stray
nodes.summary: Loudly reports any shard that died without sending its tallies — a load error or the emulator taking the process down — printing its raw output in full, since its tests are missing from the counts above.

nodes.name: load_timings
nodes.summary: Reads the per-file timings cache, treating anything unreadable, malformed or from a future format version as simply absent — a timings cache must never be able to break a test run.

nodes.name: save_timings
nodes.summary: Merges this run's observed per-file times into the cache under exponential smoothing and writes it back, so one run under unusual load cannot dictate the next week's split.

nodes.name: shard_main
nodes.summary: The child entry point: opens the control fd, requires only this shard's slice of the suite, and registers a named minitest extension that clears the default reporters and installs the streaming one before autorun's at_exit fires.

nodes.name: preview.rb
nodes.summary: Turns a run of a program into a picture you can watch: runs it on the reference interpreter, captures the screen at each frame, and writes a self-contained HTML page that plays them back. Exists because a passing test proves a feature is correct but does not let you SEE it, and motion — scrolling, parallax, animation — cannot be shown in a single screenshot at all. No emulator, no external files.
nodes.languageNotes: Hooks the interpreter's per-vblank callback to grab each settled frame, then encodes each as a PNG with Ruby's built-in zlib and inlines them as data URIs, so the page needs nothing but a browser.

nodes.name: Preview
nodes.summary: Module of singleton methods covering the whole path from a program to a watchable page: capture, PNG encoding, HTML assembly, and the command-line front end that loads an example by name.

nodes.name: self.capture
nodes.summary: Runs a program on the reference interpreter for a number of frames, optionally supplying held buttons per frame, and collects each settled frame's pixels. The frame count is the stop condition; the step budget only guards one frame against a loop that never comes round.

nodes.name: self.write
nodes.summary: Writes the assembled HTML page to a path and returns it.

nodes.name: self.html
nodes.summary: Assembles the page: every frame inlined as a PNG data URI plus a few lines of script that flip through them on a canvas at the requested speed, scaled up crisply. Returns a full document, or just the body content when a host supplies its own head.

nodes.name: self.png_data_uri
nodes.summary: Encodes one captured frame as a PNG and base64s it into a data URI for inlining in the page.

nodes.name: self.png
nodes.summary: Encodes a frame's 15-bit console colors as a minimal RGB PNG using Ruby's built-in zlib — signature, IHDR, deflated filtered scanlines, IEND — so no image gem is needed.

nodes.name: self.load_example
nodes.summary: Loads examples/NAME.rb and resolves its module by camel-casing the file name, raising a clear error when the file is missing or the module exposes no `.program` for the preview to run.

nodes.name: self.run_cli
nodes.summary: The command-line path: loads the named example, captures it with the requested frames and held keys, and writes the page to a default or given output path.

layers.name: Public API & Build Pipeline
layers.description: The `RubyGBA.build` / `RubyGBA.game` facade, the `ruby_gba.rb` barrel that requires the rest of the library, and the Thor CLI that builds, inspects and profiles a ROM from the command line.

layers.name: DSL Verb Surface
layers.description: The flat vocabulary a game author writes inside a build block — one concern module per area (drawing, sprites, sound, music, text, input, scenes, collision, tiled, layers, composition, timers) plus the effect packs that contribute verbs such as `pulse` and `shake_screen`; every verb builds an IR node rather than emitting code.

layers.name: Author-Facing Handles & Domain Models
layers.description: The objects the verbs hand back to the game author — Value, Condition, Branch, List, Table, Pool, Grid, Box, Sprite, HardwareSprite, Background, Timer, Sample, Instrument — together with the shared models for colour, sound, music, direction and fixed-point numbers that carry the expression DSL.

layers.name: Asset Import
layers.description: The boundary where art and audio on disk become in-memory data the DSL can name: PNG decoding through an ImageMagick adapter, native `.aseprite` parsing, WAV conversion, and the bitmap font model with its built-in font registry.

layers.name: IR Core
layers.description: The deliberately target-agnostic op-tree the DSL builds — `IR::Node`, the `Build` constructors and the node catalogue — plus the analyses that live here precisely because every backend must agree on the answer: palette, parity, portability, stacking, tile-map and the tree verifier.

layers.name: Guardrails & Validation
layers.description: One validator per known GBA footgun, turning what would be a silent black screen into a plain-language build error, plus the finished-ROM validator and the shared teaching-error vocabulary the messages are written in.

layers.name: Lowering Backends & ROM Assembly
layers.description: The two consumers of the same IR that must agree — the GBA backend lowering to ARM7 machine code and the Reference backend interpreting it in Ruby as a headless oracle — alongside ARM7TDMI instruction encoding, the hardware register map and cartridge assembly.

layers.name: Measurement & Developer Tooling
layers.description: Runs a built ROM in the emulator and reports where its frames went, tearing, flicker and tick rate; the routine profile it persists is read back by the next build to decide which routines get the console fast memory, so measurement feeds into the build rather than only following it. Also emitted-code regression baselines, parallel test running and asset generators.

layers.name: Example Games & Demos
layers.description: Runnable programs written against the DSL — the two flagship showcases (bitmap-mode `breakout`, tiled-mode `pacman`) plus focused demos for raycasting, parallax, sprite pools, audio and text, and the assets they draw from.

layers.name: Project Infrastructure & Documentation
layers.description: Gem packaging and dependency manifests, the Rake task graph that runs the suites, the GitHub Actions workflow, the commit-message hook, and the README and license that front the project.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start at the README, which states the project's north star: you should need to know Ruby, not the Game Boy Advance hardware. It lays out the design pillars the rest of this tour follows — hide the machine, turn footguns into friendly build errors, keep the intermediate representation target-agnostic — and catalogues the example games that demonstrate every verb. Read it as the map, then follow the pipeline it describes: an author's Ruby block becomes an IR tree, gets checked, and is lowered into a real ARM7 cartridge.

tour.title: The Build Pipeline
tour.description: `lib/ruby_gba.rb` is the single entry point: it requires the whole library in dependency order and defines `RubyGBA.build`, the one call that runs a DSL block, verifies the resulting tree, applies the guardrails, lowers it and assembles the ROM. `game.rb` records a declared-but-unbuilt game so the caller owns the output path, and `evaluated_game.rb` is the one place a DSL block actually becomes a program, so those steps cannot drift between callers. With a fan-out of 59 and a fan-in of 38, this file is both the barrel every part is reached through and the façade every part reaches back to.
tour.languageLesson: Ruby gems conventionally expose one barrel file at `lib/<gem_name>.rb` that `require`s everything else. Here that barrel also holds the public module method, so `require "ruby_gba"` gives you both the code and the API in one step.

tour.title: A Deliberately Thin Builder
tour.description: `Builder` is the object a DSL block is evaluated against, and it is thin on purpose: it includes 18 concern modules, one per area, and each supplies a slice of the flat verb surface. Drawing owns `pixel` and `fill_rect`, variables owns `var` and `approach`, control flow owns `game_loop` and `repeat`, sprites owns the single `sprite` verb that produces a software or hardware sprite depending on the screen. The rule that makes this work is that every verb builds an IR node and returns — not one of them emits machine code, which is why the whole surface can be reorganised without touching a backend.
tour.languageLesson: Ruby modules mixed in with `include` compose a flat method surface from many files. Each concern is a plain module of instance methods, so the verbs a game author calls all land on one object while the source stays split by subject.

tour.title: Handles and the Expression DSL
tour.description: The verbs from Step 3 hand back handles, and `Value` is the central one: a variable, literal or arithmetic expression that ordinary Ruby operators build bigger IR nodes out of. Comparing two Values gives a `Condition` rather than a Ruby boolean, and `.then` on it opens a `Branch` that an optional `.else` completes — so `(hp < 20).then { ... }` reads like Ruby and compiles like a jump. `Fraction` carries the fixed-point scale through arithmetic so a Float written anywhere in the program is the only place an author declares it, and `Pool` desugars a component with named fields onto parallel lists that can never fall out of step.
tour.languageLesson: Ruby lets a class redefine `+`, `>`, `&` and `|`, which is what turns arithmetic into tree construction here. The trap this exploits and then guards: every Ruby object is truthy, so a `Condition` dropped into a native `if` would silently run its body — `Condition` registers itself as pending at birth precisely so that mistake can be reported.

tour.title: Asset Import
tour.description: This is the boundary where art and audio on disk become data the DSL can name. `Image` loads and slices picture files through a swappable adapter and marks see-through pixels, while the ImageMagick adapter is the one piece that shells out to an external tool and knows nothing about the console's colour format. `Aseprite` reads the native binary format directly — compositing layers, inflating zlib cel data, keeping each artist-named animation — and `Wav` walks a RIFF container down to the 8-bit mono samples the audio hardware plays. `Font` completes the set with glyphs that each carry their own width, so a proportional font advances by the glyph rather than a fixed grid.

tour.title: The IR Op-Tree
tour.description: Here is what every verb in Step 3 was actually building. `IR::Node` defines the behaviour all nodes share — children, parent links, walking, structural equality — and is plain Ruby data with no output buffer anywhere, which is exactly what lets a program be built, inspected and checked entirely in memory before any lowering pass exists. `nodes.rb` declares roughly ninety kinds in three lines each, `build.rb` gives readable constructors so callers name a kind and its operands, and `verifier.rb` mechanically enforces the value model rather than trusting each verb to remember it. Read `ir.rb` for the comment explaining why this tree stays target-agnostic: it describes what the program does, never how one machine runs it.
tour.languageLesson: Declaring one small class per node kind, rather than a generic bag of attributes, buys you Ruby's own error reporting: asking a `pixel` node for a width it does not have raises NoMethodError at the line that asked, instead of returning a nil that travels three passes before it breaks something.

tour.title: Analyses Every Backend Shares
tour.description: These five passes live in the IR core rather than in a backend, and the reason is the same for each: every backend must agree on the answer. `Palette` collects the colours a program actually draws and assigns indexed slots, keeping the promise that an author writes colour names and never learns about palettes. `Parity` proves whether a computed value is always even, `Portability` tags each node kind portable or hardware-only, `Stacking` turns a declared layer stack into one drawing order, and `TileMap` decides which grid size a background wraps at. Each is a fact about the program, not about the machine — which is the test for whether something belongs here.

tour.title: Guardrails: Footguns as Errors
tour.description: This is the teaching mission expressed as code. `guardrails.rb` holds the mechanism — a registry of checks, the Finding/Fix/Report value objects they report through, and the Validator that runs all 27 over the tree from Step 6 before it is lowered. The four checks shown here are representative: a game loop that never waits for vertical blank ("my game runs way too fast"), the `flags |= MASK` slip that rebinds a Ruby local while the game's variable stays untouched, a bitmap draw on a tiled screen that costs time and changes nothing, and a program declaring more state than the console physically has. Every one of these would otherwise be a silent black screen; each instead names what happened and what to change.

tour.title: The GBA Lowering Backend
tour.description: The first of the two backends that consume the tree. `backends/gba.rb` wires up every collaborator, runs the prepare passes that place backgrounds, tiles, sprite art and palettes into video memory, then walks the IR emitting ARM7TDMI code in two passes — labels recorded first, branch placeholders resolved second, which is what makes forward references possible at all. `lowering.rb` dispatches a node through kind-keyed hashes instead of a case statement so two collaborators can each handle the other's kinds without depending on each other; `emit.rb` is the byte emitter nearly everything else leans on, and `memory.rb` allocates the console's fast 32K from both ends because a variable near the base costs two instructions where one further out costs four.
tour.languageLesson: Two-pass assembly is the standard answer to forward references: pass one emits instructions and records where each label landed plus every hole that needs one, pass two fills the holes in with the now-known distances. It replaces hand-rolled branch-offset arithmetic, which is the classic source of off-by-one bugs in a code generator.

tour.title: ARM Encoding and ROM Assembly
tour.description: The bottom of the stack, where the pipeline finally produces bytes. `asm.rb` encodes ARMv4T instructions as raw 32-bit little-endian words — only the subset the DSL needs, plus helpers answering whether a word clobbers a given register, which the register conventions in Step 9 depend on. `rom.rb` manages the cartridge buffer and writes the header the BIOS insists on (Nintendo logo, title, fixed byte, entry branch, complement checksum, power-of-two padding), and `rom_validator.rb` then checks the finished image for exactly the structural faults that make real hardware or an accurate emulator refuse to boot. `constants.rb` is what lets all of this name a register instead of an address.
tour.languageLesson: A GBA cartridge header carries a complement checksum over bytes 0xA0-0xBC: the BIOS refuses to boot an image whose checksum byte does not match. It is a deliberate integrity gate, not an error-detection code, which is why a ROM builder must compute it after the title and codes are written and never before.

tour.title: Two Oracles for One Tree
tour.description: The second backend is what keeps the first honest. `Backends::Reference` runs the same IR directly in Ruby against simulated hardware — a fake screen, a fake gamepad, an in-memory variable store, timers and a voice mixer — so a program's logic and its visible pixels can be asserted in-process with no ROM and no emulator. Its framebuffer models the real quirks that matter (dropped out-of-bounds writes, the two-page tear-free screen, camera, fade and tint applied on read-back) and its list value matches the console on capacity and on what a too-large value reads back as. `emulator.rb` is the single seam to the real emulator and `verifier.rb` the counterpart oracle that runs a finished ROM headlessly and reads back actual rendered pixels — a feature is only done when both backends agree.

tour.title: Measurement Feeds the Build
tour.description: This is where the pipeline stops being a straight line. `Profiler` runs a finished cartridge on the emulator from Step 11, samples the program counter and maps addresses back onto named routines — nothing is predicted, every number is a count of what happened. `RoutineProfile` then persists those counts keyed by routine *name*, so they survive a rebuild where addresses would not, and the next build reads them back to decide which routines get the console's fast 32K memory. `Tearing` and `TickRate` measure the two failures a build-time estimate cannot decide: whether the display showed a row before the game finished painting it, and whether a timer handler silently lost ticks it had no queue for.

tour.title: Command Line and Tooling
tour.description: The developer-facing surface around everything above. `cli.rb` is a Thor command set — `build` compiles a game file to a cartridge or dumps its IR, `profile` reports where frames went, `inspect` disassembles, `new` scaffolds — reached through the thin `bin/ruby-gba` shim. `tools/preview.rb` answers a problem tests cannot: it runs a program on the reference interpreter, captures every frame and writes a self-contained HTML page that plays them back, because motion like scrolling or parallax cannot be shown in one screenshot. `emitted_baseline.rb` and its checked-in JSON record every example's emitted size and fail on any growth, so the diff of that file is where a reviewer sees what a feature cost.
tour.languageLesson: Thor maps CLI subcommands onto plain Ruby methods, with `desc`/`option` declarations generating the help text — the same pattern Rails and Bundler use. Pairing it with a one-line `bin/` shim that only adjusts `$LOAD_PATH` keeps the executable trivial and the logic testable.

tour.title: Examples Are the Curriculum
tour.description: In a teaching framework the examples are not an afterthought — each one exists to demonstrate specific verbs, and reading them is how the DSL is actually learned. `snake.rb` is the README's worked example (a `list` for the growing body, `every` for the beat, `save_var` for a high score that survives power-off), while `breakout.rb` and `pacman.rb` are the two flagship showcases for the bitmap and tiled screens respectively. `raycaster.rb` proves the fractional-number design carries real weight with a first-person view built from build-time tables and a perspective divide, and `shmup.rb` is the worked example for splitting a game across files with `layers` naming the stack once and scenes owning what they draw.

tour.title: Build, Test and CI
tour.description: The capstone that ties the whole tour together mechanically. The `Rakefile` compiles the emulator's C extension as a cached file task and defines both the serial and the parallel suites, plus the tasks for the emitted-code baselines from Step 13 and the HTML previews. The `Gemfile` keeps the emulator a development-only path dependency, so consumers of the library never need a C compiler or libmgba — the framework itself is pure Ruby, and only the test harness is not. The CI workflow runs the three checks that correspond to the three things this project claims: the Ruby suite, the headless-emulator suite that verifies real pixels, and the size baseline that catches silent growth.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions YAML uses `on` for triggers, `jobs` for parallelism and `steps` for sequence. Note the `if: always()` idiom used to upload logs even when an earlier step failed — without it, artifacts are skipped exactly on the runs where you most need to read them.
